# Hotel price discrimination by location: how it really works

Hotels sell to each country differently. Here is what that means, why a VPN alone rarely changes the price, and how to use market pricing to pay less.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/hotel-price-discrimination-by-location.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: Hidden prices

## Key takeaways

- Hotel price discrimination by location means selling the same hotel at different prices depending on the market where the booking is made.
- Changing only your IP address on the same site usually moves the price of the same rate very little.
- Real differences come from market-targeted rates, local sellers, local promotions and member pricing that differ by country.
- Resident-only rates are not a saving for visitors; compare final totals with taxes, fees and currency included.
- Arbitrica searches the same hotel from 195 countries at checkout and validates the identical hotel with all taxes and fees.

Price discrimination sounds sinister, but in economics it is a neutral term: selling the same product to different customers at different prices. Airlines do it with fare classes, software companies do it with country pricing, and hotels do it by market. If you have ever seen the same hotel at different prices when booked from different countries, you have seen hotel price discrimination by location.

What most people get wrong is the mechanism. The common story is that a booking site reads your IP address and raises the price. The reality is more interesting, and more useful if you want to pay less.

## What price discrimination by location means for hotels

The travel industry calls it pricing by point of sale: the market where the booking is made. A hotel decides how it wants to sell to travelers from each country. It may offer a promotion to one market, sell through tour operators in another and leave a third to the big booking sites. Each of those decisions creates a different set of offers for the same hotel, depending on where the booking is made.

The price difference therefore comes from what is on offer in each country: different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions.

> Chart: Different countries get different inventory, channels, local rates, promotions and currencies, and pricing algorithms move rates all day.

## Hotel prices by IP address: what actually happens

If you open the same hotel on the same site and change only your IP address, the price for the same rate usually moves very little, if at all. Travelers who test this with a VPN are often disappointed for exactly that reason. The real differences appear when changing countries changes what you can book:

- **Market-targeted rates.** Booking sites let hotels create rates that are offered only to travelers booking from specific countries. These rates sit next to the standard rate and appear only in their target markets.

- **Local sellers.** In many countries, local online agencies, tour operators and travel portals sell hotel stays from wholesale inventory. They do not show up in a search from your own country, but they can be cheaper for the identical hotel.

- **Local promotions.** Payment partners, banks and local campaigns run discounts in one country and not in others.

- **Member pricing by market.** Loyalty and member discounts are not offered the same way in every country.

- **Currency and tax display.** Prices set in local currency drift with exchange rates, and some countries show totals with taxes while others add them at the end. Part of what looks like discrimination is just display.

That is also why the VPN method has limits, which we cover in [VPN vs Arbitrica for hotel booking](https://arbitrica.com/blog/vpn-vs-arbitrica-hotel-booking.html). The saving comes from finding the offers that exist in other countries.

## How large location-based price differences get

In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler's own country, with a typical gap of 20-40%. A 2024 NordVPN study found that travel bookings made through US websites came out up to 70% higher than through websites elsewhere (its largest gap was a car rental). One of its examples was a seven-night stay in a triple room at a Milan hotel for a family of three: about $1,216 searched from the US and $1,012 searched from Italy.

> Chart: 2024 NordVPN study: a seven-night stay in a triple room at a Milan hotel for a family of three cost about $1,216 searched from the US and $1,012 searched from Italy.

The country with the lowest price is not fixed. It changes from hotel to hotel and from week to week, as promotions start and end and as local demand moves.

## Why hotel prices vary by country

Hotels have ordinary business reasons for pricing differently by market.

### Feeder markets and seasons

Every hotel has markets that send most of its guests and markets it wants to grow. School holidays, public holidays and travel seasons fall at different times in different countries, so a hotel may push a discount toward a market whose travelers book during its quiet weeks.

### Distribution contracts

Hotels sign deals with wholesalers and tour operators who buy inventory at negotiated rates and resell it in their own countries, often inside packages. Those rates follow their own rules and are not always matched on the big global sites.

### Competition and purchasing power

What travelers from a given country are used to paying, and how many alternatives they see, influences how a hotel prices for that market. This is the reason behind "book from a cheaper country" advice. It is only one factor, though, and often not the decisive one, as the guide to the [cheapest country to book hotels from](https://arbitrica.com/blog/cheapest-country-to-book-hotels-from.html) explains.

### Parity rules

For years, large booking sites used parity clauses that limited how much lower a hotel could price elsewhere. Several European countries restricted those clauses, and since Booking.com was designated a gatekeeper under the EU Digital Markets Act in 2024, it can no longer impose them in the EU. Looser parity gives hotels more scope to price differently by channel and market.

## Where location-based price differences come from

| Source of the difference | How it works | Can a traveler from another country book it? |

| Market-targeted rate | The hotel offers a rate only to bookings made from certain countries | Usually yes, when booked from that country |

| Local agency or wholesaler | A seller in another country resells inventory bought at negotiated rates | Often yes, check the seller and the terms |

| Resident-only rate | Local residents get a discount, sometimes checked at arrival | No, unless you are a resident |

| Currency difference | Rate set in local currency moves with the exchange rate | Yes, watch card fees and conversion |

| Tax display | Price shown with or without taxes and fees | Not a real saving, compare final totals |

| Same site, IP change only | Same rate, same seller, different connection | Usually little or no change in price |

## Is it legal and fair?

Pricing by market is common in travel and across many industries, and booking a rate that is openly offered is a normal purchase. The rules that matter to you are the rate conditions: if a rate is limited to residents of a country, the hotel can ask for proof at check-in.

Inside the European Union, the 2018 Geo-blocking Regulation limits traders from applying different general conditions, including prices, to customers from other EU countries purely because of their nationality or place of residence, and hotel accommodation is one of the services it covers. Outside the EU, rules vary.

## How to use location-based pricing to pay less

- **Fix your baseline**Start with the exact hotel, dates, guests and rate type, and note the final total with taxes and fees.

- **Search from other countries**Search the same hotel from other countries, including local sellers where you can, not only the same global site.

- **Skip resident-only rates**Leave them out unless you qualify.

- **Compare totals**Compare after taxes, fees and currency conversion.

- **Prefer free cancellation**The lowest country today may not be the lowest next week, so keep the option to rebook.

The hard part is coverage. There are 195 countries, the lowest price moves between them, and checking more than a handful by hand is impractical.

## How Arbitrica handles location-based pricing

Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that shows up at checkout, searches the same hotel from 195 countries and finds the lowest price on Earth for it at a different provider than the one you are on. It validates that the offer is for the identical hotel with all taxes and fees included, and prepares the booking so you only review and pay. Arbitrica's approach also repeats the search after you book, until the free cancellation window ends, and confirms any new booking before the original is cancelled.

> Chart: At checkout Arbitrica searches the same item from 195 countries, checks it is identical with all taxes and fees included, and prepares everything at the lowest price.

The same hotel is often 5 to 30 percent cheaper when booked from somewhere else. Research showed that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking with Arbitrica, and up to $3,000 a year. Arbitrica also serves companies: teams traveling to trade shows and conferences, and the operations and travel managers who book for them. The same market-by-market pricing shows up in flights, event tickets and online shopping, and the same mechanisms apply there.

For more background, read [what geographic price arbitrage is](https://arbitrica.com/blog/what-is-geographic-price-arbitrage.html), the guide to [hidden hotel prices](https://arbitrica.com/blog/hidden-hotel-prices-guide.html) and the [hotel price tracker](https://arbitrica.com/hotel-price-tracker.html) page.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is hotel price discrimination by location?

It is the practice of selling the same hotel at different prices depending on the market where the booking is made. It happens through market-targeted rates, local sellers, local promotions and member pricing that differ by country.

### Do hotel prices change by IP address?

On the same site, changing only your IP address usually moves the price of the same rate very little. Real differences come from the different rates and sellers available when you search from another country.

### Why do hotel prices vary by country?

Hotels sell to each market differently: they target promotions at certain countries, sell through local agencies and wholesalers, and react to local seasons and competition. Currency and tax display add further differences.

### Is it legal to book a hotel rate offered in another country?

Booking a rate that is openly offered is a normal purchase. Check the rate conditions, because some rates are limited to residents and the hotel can ask for proof at check-in.

# Hotel price drops after booking: why they happen

The price you paid was right for that moment, but the market kept moving. Here is why hotels get cheaper after you book and how to turn a drop into money earned.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/hotel-price-drop-after-booking.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: Save money

## Key takeaways

- Hotel prices keep changing between the day you book and the day you check in, in both directions.
- With free cancellation you can book the identical hotel again at the lower price and then cancel the original.
- Always make the new booking first and cancel the original only once the new one is confirmed.
- A price drop over time and a lower price from another country can add up on the same booking.
- Arbitrica's approach repeats the search from 195 countries after you book, until free cancellation ends.

You book a hotel, feel good about the price and move on to planning the rest of the trip. A week later you look at the same hotel again and the price has dropped by $40 a night. It happens often, and it is not random. Once you understand why hotel prices fall after booking, you can turn those drops into money earned.

## How often do hotel prices drop after booking?

Hotel prices change frequently between the day you book and the day you check in. How often a specific hotel gets cheaper depends on the destination, the season and how far ahead you book, but some patterns are well known:

- Bookings made well in advance leave more time for the price to move, in either direction.

- Hotels in competitive cities with many nearby alternatives adjust prices more often.

- Shoulder seasons, just before or after peak periods, tend to be the most volatile.

> Chart: Illustrative: the price of the same hotel keeps moving after you book. A drop before free cancellation ends can be rebooked.

## Why hotel prices drop after you book

Hotel pricing is dynamic. Revenue management systems adjust rates based on occupancy forecasts, competitor prices, day-of-week patterns and demand signals from searches and bookings. The guide to [how hotel dynamic pricing works](https://arbitrica.com/blog/how-hotel-dynamic-pricing-works.html) goes deeper into these systems.

When a hotel is filling more slowly than forecast, the system lowers prices to stimulate demand. When a group cancels a large block of rooms, prices can drop to fill the sudden inventory. When a competing hotel cuts its rate, the system may match it.

These adjustments can happen daily or even several times a day. The price you paid was right for that moment, but the market kept moving.

## The free cancellation opportunity

Many hotel bookings come with free cancellation until a day or two before check-in. That creates a simple opportunity: if the price for the identical hotel drops after you book, you can make a new booking at the lower price and cancel the original. You stay at the same hotel on the same dates.

Make the new booking first and cancel the original only once the new one is confirmed. Before you cancel, check that the new booking is for the same hotel and room type, that the new price includes all taxes and fees, and that cancelling the original booking really is free.

The catch is the effort. Checking a booking once a day for 30 days means 30 manual searches for a single hotel, and more for every additional trip.

## Which bookings can be rebooked

Whether a drop is useful to you depends on the terms of the booking you already hold.

| Booking type | Can you rebook at a lower price? | What to watch |

| Free cancellation, pay at the hotel | Yes, until the cancellation deadline | Deadlines are often set in the hotel's local time |

| Free cancellation, prepaid | Yes, until the cancellation deadline | The refund can take a few days to reach your card, so both charges may show for a while |

| Partly refundable | Only if the drop is bigger than the cancellation fee | Subtract the fee before you count the saving |

| Non-refundable | Usually no | The lower headline price at booking removes your chance to benefit later |

This is why a refundable rate that costs a little more on day one is often the better deal for trips more than a few weeks away.

## How to rebook a hotel at a lower price

- **Note your booking details**Write down the hotel, dates, guests, room type, meal plan, total paid and the exact cancellation deadline.

- **Search the identical hotel again**Check the same dates and terms every few days, and more often close to the deadline.

- **Compare the final total**Compare totals with all taxes and fees included, not the nightly rate.

- **Book the new rate first**Wait for the confirmation of the new booking before you touch the old one.

- **Cancel the original**Cancel before the deadline and keep the cancellation confirmation.

For a longer walkthrough, see [how to rebook a hotel at a lower price](https://arbitrica.com/blog/rebook-hotel-at-lower-price.html).

## Mistakes that wipe out a hotel price drop

Most failed rebookings come from a small number of avoidable slips:

- **Cancelling first.** If you cancel before the new booking is confirmed, the lower rate can disappear while you are paying, and you may lose the hotel altogether on busy dates.

- **Comparing different rooms.** A lower price for a smaller room type, or a rate without breakfast, is not the same booking.

- **Missing a fee.** Resort fees, city taxes and payment fees can be added late in the booking flow. A drop in the nightly rate that is eaten by a new fee is not a drop.

- **Misreading the deadline.** Cancellation deadlines are often set in the hotel's local time, which can be hours earlier than you expect.

- **Switching to non-refundable.** Rebooking into a non-refundable rate ends your chance to benefit from the next drop. Keep the new booking flexible if you can.

## Price drops over time and across countries

A price drop over time is one source of savings. Another is geographic: the same hotel is often 5-30% cheaper when searched from another country, because different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions. The two can add up. A hotel that falls from $300 to $260 a night over a few weeks may at the same time be available for less when searched from another country.

> Chart: Geographic arbitrage (other countries, at checkout) and time arbitrage (later moments, after you pay).

Many price trackers only watch for drops on the price you can see from your own country. Arbitrica combines both: geographic arbitrage, which searches the same hotel from 195 countries, and time arbitrage, which repeats that search at many points in time. [Time arbitrage explained](https://arbitrica.com/blog/time-arbitrage-explained.html) covers the second mechanism in detail.

## How Arbitrica captures price drops

Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that lives in your browser. At checkout, it searches the same hotel from 195 countries in real time and finds the lowest price on Earth at a different provider than the one you are on. This is live arbitrage.

After you book, Arbitrica's approach repeats the search until the free-cancellation window ends. This is multiple-time arbitrage. When the identical hotel becomes available at a lower price with all taxes and fees included, the mechanism Arbitrica developed prepares a re-booking at that price. The new booking is confirmed before the original booking is cancelled. Before anything is prepared, Arbitrica checks that the lower price will not suddenly change.

Research showed that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking with Arbitrica, and up to $3,000 a year. In one real booking, a hotel was offered on Booking for $1,527.39 and Arbitrica found the identical hotel for $1,180.27, earning the user $347.12 (23%).

## Beyond hotels

Price drops after purchase are not unique to hotels. Flights, car rentals, event tickets, pre-orders and delayed-shipment online purchases, and subscriptions all have prices that move and often a cancellation or return window. The same approach applies: search again over time, and from other countries, until that window closes. Arbitrica also serves companies: teams traveling to trade shows and conferences, and the operations and travel managers who book for them.

## Frequently asked questions

### Why did my hotel price drop after I booked?

Hotel revenue management systems keep adjusting rates after you book, based on occupancy, competitor prices and demand. If the hotel fills more slowly than forecast, prices often fall.

### Can I get the lower price if my hotel gets cheaper?

Yes, if your booking has free cancellation. Book the identical hotel at the lower price, wait for the confirmation, then cancel the original before the deadline.

### Is it worth booking a refundable rate?

For trips more than a few weeks away, usually yes. A refundable rate lets you rebook if the price drops, and one drop often covers the small premium.

### How often should I check my hotel price after booking?

Every few days is a reasonable habit, and more often close to the cancellation deadline. Arbitrica's approach repeats the search for you until free cancellation ends.

# The hotel price tracker that searches from 195 countries

Hotel prices vary in two directions. They vary by place, because each country gets different rates. They also vary over time, because rates move as demand, cancellations and inventory change between the day you book and the day you check in. Arbitrica is built around both.

## How to track a hotel price by hand

If you want to try it yourself first, this routine catches the most common drops:

- **Book a refundable rate**Free cancellation is what lets a later, lower price become money you earn. Note the deadline and the hotel's time zone.

- **Record the full total**Write down the final amount with taxes and fees, the rate name and what is included, such as breakfast.

- **Set reminders**Check again a month out, two weeks out and a few days before the cancellation deadline.

- **Compare like for like**Same hotel, dates, guests and rate conditions. A non-refundable rate is a different booking.

- **Book first, then cancel**Only cancel the original once the new booking is confirmed.

This works for one trip. It gets hard with several trips, and it still only covers your own country. The guide to [hotel price drops after booking](https://arbitrica.com/blog/hotel-price-drop-after-booking.html) covers the manual method in more detail.

## When tracking pays off most

- **International hotels**, where local distribution and country-specific promotions widen the gap between countries.

- **Bookings made weeks ahead**, which leave a long window for the price to move.

- **Shoulder seasons**, when hotels adjust rates often to fill nights.

- **Longer and more expensive stays**, where the same percentage is a bigger amount.

- **Team travel** to trade shows and conferences, where many bookings move together. Arbitrica also serves companies, including the operations managers and travel managers who book for them.

TipTracking does nothing for a non-refundable rate after you pay. If a trip is more than a few weeks away, a flexible rate that costs a little more on day one often ends up the better deal.

## Price alerts versus a tracker that acts

Many trackers stop at an alert. You get an email saying the rate dropped, and the rest is up to you: find the identical hotel at the new price, check that taxes and fees are included, read the cancellation terms, book again and cancel the original before the deadline. Plenty of people mean to do it and never do, and the lower price is lost.

Alerts also tend to watch one site from one country. If the lower price is on another site, or only available when the hotel is searched from another country, an alert from your own country never fires. Arbitrica's approach covers both gaps: the search runs from 195 countries, and when a lower price for the identical hotel appears, the new booking is prepared for you to review and pay, then confirmed before the original is cancelled.

A hotel price tracker watches the price of a hotel for you and finds a lower price for the same hotel, at checkout or after you book. Arbitrica searches the same hotel from 195 countries and repeats the search until free cancellation ends.

### Does hotel price tracking work on non-refundable bookings?

Only before you pay. After a non-refundable booking, a lower price cannot be used because cancelling would forfeit the original payment.

### Will I be left without a hotel if a rebooking fails?

No. The new booking is confirmed first, and only then is the original cancelled. If the lower price is gone, the original booking stays as it is.

### Does Arbitrica only track hotel prices?

No. The same mechanisms apply to online shopping such as Amazon, flights, car rentals, event tickets and subscriptions.

# Do hotel prices change by IP address?

The same hotel can cost less when you search from another country. The reason is what each country has access to, not a price tag on your connection.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/hotel-prices-by-ip-address.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: Hidden prices

## Key takeaways

- What changes the hotel price you can get is mostly the country you search from, not your IP address as such.
- Different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates, promotions and currencies for the same hotel.
- In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler's own country.
- A 2024 NordVPN investigation found a Milan stay at about $1,216 searched from the US and $1,012 searched from Italy.
- Arbitrica searches the same hotel from 195 countries at checkout and validates it is identical with all taxes and fees included.

Search for the same hotel from two different countries and you can get two different prices. That leads many travelers to a simple theory: booking sites look at your IP address and charge you accordingly. The real picture is more useful. What changes the price you can get is mostly the country you search from, because different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates, promotions and currencies. Your IP address is simply how a search gets placed in a country.

## Do hotel prices change by IP address?

The short answer: what the evidence points to is the country you search from, not the connection itself. A search made from another country can reach offers that a search from your own country does not. Those offers can be for the very same hotel, on the same dates, with the same room, and they can be lower.

That distinction matters for what you do next. If prices were simply set by IP, any IP in any country would do. Because the difference comes from what each country has access to, the country you pick matters, the result varies from hotel to hotel, and the only way to find the lowest price is to search the same hotel from many countries and check that the offers are truly identical.

## Why the same hotel has a different price in a different country

A hotel rarely sells all its rooms through one price list. It distributes them through many routes, and many of those routes are tied to particular countries.

> Chart: Different countries get different inventory, channels, local rates, promotions and currencies, and pricing algorithms move rates all day.

- **Inventory.** Hotels allocate rooms to different partners, and some partners only sell in certain countries. A search from one country can see allocations a search from another country never reaches.

- **Channels.** Travel sites, wholesalers, tour operators and local agencies each have their own contracts with the hotel. The set of channels that answer a search differs by country.

- **Local rates.** Some rates are built for a domestic market, such as rates for residents of a country or for travelers booking in a local currency.

- **Promotions.** Sites and hotels run campaigns aimed at specific countries, and a promotion running in one market may not run in yours.

- **Currency.** A price quoted in another currency is converted at a rate set by the site or your card issuer, and that conversion can move the final total either way.

Put together, these routes mean the same hotel can come in at several prices at the same moment. The article on [hotel price differences by location](https://arbitrica.com/blog/hotel-price-discrimination-by-location.html) looks at this in more depth.

## What the research shows

In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler's own country, and the typical gap was 20-40%.

An independent investigation points the same way. In April 2024, NordVPN commissioned an external agency to run simultaneous searches for identical travel products from the same vendors through servers in several countries. It reported that travel bookings made through US websites came out up to 70% higher than through websites elsewhere (its largest gap was a car rental). One example was a seven-night stay in Milan for a family of three: about $1,216 searched from the US and $1,012 searched from Italy. NordVPN sells VPNs, so it has an interest in the result, and the study covered a small set of specific bookings, but the pattern matches what travelers report.

> Chart: 2024 NordVPN study: a seven-night stay in a triple room at a Milan hotel for a family of three cost about $1,216 searched from the US and $1,012 searched from Italy.

The size of the gap changes with the hotel, the dates and the countries involved. Some hotels show almost no difference; others show a large one. There is no single country that is always lowest, which is why the list of [cheapest countries to book hotels from](https://arbitrica.com/blog/cheapest-country-to-book-hotels-from.html) is a starting point rather than a rule.

## Cookies, logged-in pricing and your device

Location is not the only thing that can change what you see. A well-known 2014 Northeastern University study tested 16 e-commerce and travel sites with real and simulated users. Among its travel findings, it reported that two travel sites offered reduced hotel prices to members, that some sites showed different results to some users, and that one site personalized results for mobile users. Another site reordered results based on users' click and purchase history, which the researchers did not count as price steering because the order did not track price.

Membership programs are the clearest case today. Booking.com's Genius program gives signed-in members discounts at participating properties, and Expedia's terms refer to Member Prices that are separate from prices available to the general public. If you compare a price while signed in with one while signed out, you are comparing two different offers.

TipTo test whether your own history affects what you see, run the same search in a private window and in your normal browser, with the same sign-in state. Treat member discounts as a separate offer, and compare totals with all taxes and fees included.

The study's travel findings were about member rates, devices and the order of results. They do not show a simple rule such as "the price goes up every time you search", so clearing cookies is a reasonable check but not a strategy for finding the lowest price.

## VPN hotel booking: is it cheaper?

A VPN lets you place a search in another country, so it can open up prices you cannot get from your own country. It is how most people first discover that the same hotel can cost less elsewhere. Doing it well takes care:

- **Start clean**Use a private window and the same sign-in state for every country you test.

- **Pick countries with a reason**Try the destination country and a few others. The lowest country changes from hotel to hotel.

- **Match the offer exactly**Same hotel, dates, guests, room type, meal plan and cancellation terms.

- **Compare the full total**Go to the final payment step and convert the currency yourself, including any card fees for paying in a foreign currency.

- **Read the rate conditions**Some rates are limited to residents of a country or to particular payment methods. NordVPN's own article notes that some sites prohibit VPN use in their terms.

The bigger problem is scale. A VPN checks one country at a time, and every check means a new search, a new currency and a new set of terms to verify. Covering a handful of countries takes an evening; covering all of them is not realistic by hand. The guides to [Booking.com prices and VPNs](https://arbitrica.com/blog/booking-com-different-prices-vpn-explained.html) and [VPN versus Arbitrica for hotel booking](https://arbitrica.com/blog/vpn-vs-arbitrica-hotel-booking.html) go through the trade-offs.

> Chart: By hand, a VPN checks one country at a time. Arbitrica searches the same item from 195 countries at once.

## Searching the same hotel from 195 countries

Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that meets you at checkout. When you are about to pay for a hotel, it searches the same hotel from 195 countries, validates that it is identical with all taxes and fees included, and prepares everything at the lowest price on Earth. The lower price it finds is always at a different provider than the one you are on. You review and pay. See [how it works](https://arbitrica.com/how-it-works.html) for the full flow.

Prices also keep moving after you book. Arbitrica's approach repeats the search after you book, until free cancellation ends. When the identical hotel becomes available at a lower total, a new booking is prepared and confirmed first, and only then is the original cancelled.

The same mechanisms work for companies, such as travel managers and operations managers booking teams into trade shows and conferences, and they reach beyond hotels to flights, event tickets and online shopping. Research showed that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking with Arbitrica, and up to $3,000 a year.

## What to remember about hotel prices and location

- The country you search from changes which offers you can reach: inventory, channels, local rates, promotions and currency.

- The same hotel is often 5-30% cheaper bought from another country or at another moment.

- Member rates and sign-in state are separate offers; keep them consistent when you compare.

- A lower price only counts if the hotel, room and terms are identical and the total includes all taxes and fees.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do hotel prices change based on your IP address?

What changes is mostly the country you search from. A search from another country can reach different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions for the same hotel, and some of those offers can be lower.

### Is it cheaper to book a hotel with a VPN?

Sometimes. A VPN lets you search from another country, which can open up lower prices for the same hotel. It checks one country at a time, and you must confirm the hotel, room, terms and full total are identical.

### Do hotel sites raise prices if I search repeatedly?

Published research on travel sites found differences tied to member rates, devices and the order of results. A private window with the same sign-in state is a reasonable way to check what you see.

### Why is the same hotel cheaper from another country?

Hotels distribute rooms through many partners and channels, many tied to particular countries, and run local rates and promotions. Currency conversion also changes the final total.

# Hotels.com price guarantee: what changed and what to do now

Expedia Group ended the Hotel Price Guarantee on Hotels.com and Expedia in July 2026. Here is what still protects you and where lower prices are found.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/hotels-com-price-guarantee.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: Comparisons

## Key takeaways

- Expedia Group ended the Hotel Price Guarantee on Hotels.com and Expedia on July 28, 2026, with no replacement announced for hotels.
- Expedia's One Key Price Drop Protection covers flights booked in the Expedia app by Gold and Platinum members, not hotels.
- Booking.com still runs a price match for the same property, accommodation type, cancellation policy and dates, claimed until 24 hours before arrival.
- A price guarantee only covers what the site considers the same offer, and it does not search other providers or other countries for you.
- Arbitrica searches the same hotel from 195 countries at checkout and prepares everything at the lowest price on Earth, at a different provider.

If you are looking for the Hotels.com price guarantee, the short answer is that it no longer exists. Expedia Group ended the Hotel Price Guarantee on both Hotels.com and Expedia on July 28, 2026, and no replacement has been announced for hotels. This guide explains what the guarantee covered, what changed, which price matches still exist, and how to get a lower price for the same hotel without one.

## Does Hotels.com still have a price guarantee?

No. In June 2026, Frequent Miler reported a Hotels.com email to members that said: "We will no longer be offering Hotel Price Guarantee on Expedia or Hotels.com." AwardWallet reported the same change with an effective date of July 28, 2026, and Upgraded Points, in its coverage of the One Key changes that went live that day, wrote that both sites "have eliminated the Hotel Price Guarantee" and that "there's no replacement for it."

Hotels.com and Expedia are both owned by Expedia Group and share the One Key rewards program, which is why the change applies to both sites at once. Some older Hotels.com and Expedia help pages can still turn up in search results with guarantee wording; check the date and the current terms on the site before relying on them.

TipIf you booked before July 28, 2026 and want to make a claim, contact Hotels.com customer service directly. The public reports on the change do not describe how bookings made before that date are handled, so get the answer from Hotels.com in writing.

## What the Hotels.com price guarantee used to do

According to Upgraded Points, the Hotel Price Guarantee paid members who found a lower price after booking. Like most guarantees of this kind, it was built around a claim: you found the lower offer, submitted it, and the site checked whether it qualified before paying the difference.

That check is where most claims succeed or fail. Price guarantees across the travel industry share a few common conditions:

- The lower offer must be for the same hotel, dates, number of guests and room type.

- The cancellation policy and board, such as breakfast included, must match.

- The offer must be publicly available, so member-only, corporate and coupon rates usually do not count.

- There is a deadline for submitting the claim, often tied to check-in.

Each program writes its own version of these rules, and the site that pays the claim decides whether your offer meets them.

## What still exists after the change

The end of the Hotel Price Guarantee does not mean every price protection is gone. Here is what we could verify from published sources in October 2026:

| Program | Covers hotels? | What is reported |

| Hotels.com and Expedia Hotel Price Guarantee | Ended | Discontinued July 28, 2026, with no replacement announced (AwardWallet, Upgraded Points). |

| Expedia One Key Price Drop Protection | No, flights only | Expedia's page describes it for flights booked in the Expedia app by One Key Gold and Platinum members, with the difference paid as OneKeyCash after the trip. |

| Booking.com price match | Yes | NerdWallet, in a May 2026 update, describes claims for the same property, accommodation type, cancellation policy and dates, submitted until 24 hours before arrival. |

| Hotel chains' own best rate guarantees | Yes, for direct bookings | Many chains publish their own guarantee for bookings made on their site, each with its own conditions. |

For the full Booking.com rules and how they compare, see the guide to the [Booking.com price match](https://arbitrica.com/blog/booking-com-price-match.html). For Expedia's side of the change, see [Expedia price drop refunds](https://arbitrica.com/blog/expedia-price-drop-refund.html).

## How to claim a hotel price guarantee where one still exists

If you booked on a site or with a hotel chain that still offers a price match, the steps are similar everywhere:

- **Read the current terms**Find the guarantee page on the site you booked with and note the deadline and the exclusions.

- **Match every detail**Same hotel, dates, guests, room type, board and cancellation policy. Check the total with all taxes and fees on both offers.

- **Capture the evidence**Take screenshots of the lower offer showing the price, dates, room type and terms, with the date and time visible.

- **Submit quickly**Prices move, and if the lower offer disappears before the claim is checked, it may be rejected. On Booking.com, NerdWallet says you can claim from your reservation confirmation or through customer care.

- **Keep the reference**Save the claim number and any replies until the adjustment is applied.

## The limit of every price guarantee: "the same offer"

A price guarantee only pays when the site agrees that the lower price is for exactly the same offer. That definition is written by the site paying the claim. A different room name, a slightly different cancellation policy, a rate that requires signing in, or an offer from a site that does not reveal the hotel until after booking can each be enough to reject a claim. NerdWallet's summary of Booking.com's rules, for example, lists loyalty-only rates, offers labeled "Partner offer" and sites that do not reveal the property until after booking among the exclusions.

A guarantee also depends on you finding the lower price first. It does not search for you, and it only helps with the site you booked on. Lower prices for the same hotel are often found at other providers and from other countries, where no guarantee on your original site applies.

A price guarantee covers what a site considers the same offer. The lower price is often somewhere it does not look.

## Why the same hotel can be lower when searched from another country

Different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions. Searching the same hotel from another country can open up lower prices that you cannot get from your own country, often from a different provider.

> Chart: In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler’s own country. The typical gap was 20–40%.

In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler's own country, and the typical gap was 20-40%. Independent research points the same way: a 2024 NordVPN study found that travel bookings made through US websites came out up to 70% higher than through websites elsewhere (its largest gap was a car rental).

> Chart: 2024 NordVPN study: a seven-night stay in a triple room at a Milan hotel for a family of three cost about $1,216 searched from the US and $1,012 searched from Italy.

In that study, a seven-night stay in a triple room at a Milan hotel for a family of three cost about $1,216 searched from the US and $1,012 searched from Italy. No price guarantee would pay that difference, because the lower offer comes from a different search and, often, a different provider. The guide to [hotel prices in different countries](https://arbitrica.com/blog/booking-com-prices-different-countries.html) explains how these gaps form.

## How to get a lower price without a price guarantee

With the Hotels.com guarantee gone, two habits do the work it used to promise, and more.

### Search from other countries before you pay

By hand, this means a VPN, one country at a time, and a careful check that the hotel, room type, terms and total are identical. It is slow and covers only a few countries. Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that meets you at checkout, searches the same hotel from 195 countries, validates that it is identical with all taxes and fees included, and prepares everything at the lowest price on Earth. You review and pay. The lower price it finds is always at a different provider, so there is no claim to file and nothing to wait for. [How Arbitrica works](https://arbitrica.com/how-it-works.html) covers the process in more detail.

### Book refundable, then rebook if the price drops

A refundable booking is a guarantee you control. If the same hotel gets cheaper before the cancellation deadline, you book the lower rate, wait for confirmation and cancel the original. Our step-by-step guide on how to [rebook a hotel at a lower price](https://arbitrica.com/blog/rebook-hotel-at-lower-price.html) covers the pitfalls.

> Chart: Geographic arbitrage (other countries, at checkout) and time arbitrage (later moments, after you pay).

Arbitrica's approach repeats the search after you book, from 195 countries, until free cancellation ends. When the identical hotel becomes available at a lower price from another provider, a new booking is prepared and confirmed first, and only then is the original cancelled. Research demonstrated that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking with Arbitrica, and up to $3,000 a year.

## What this means for business travel

Travel managers and operations managers who relied on site guarantees to keep team hotel costs in check now need another safeguard. Booking refundable rates for trade shows and conferences, then searching again from other countries until the cancellation deadline, replaces a claim process with savings that do not depend on approval. Arbitrica also serves companies booking hotels for teams, and the same mechanisms apply to flights, event tickets and other purchases.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does Hotels.com still have a price guarantee?

No. Expedia Group ended the Hotel Price Guarantee on both Hotels.com and Expedia on July 28, 2026, and reports at the time said no replacement had been announced.

### Does Hotels.com price match?

Not since the Hotel Price Guarantee ended on July 28, 2026. If your booking has free cancellation, you can book the lower rate yourself and cancel the original once the new booking is confirmed.

### Does Expedia Price Drop Protection cover hotels?

No. Expedia's page describes One Key Price Drop Protection for flights booked in the Expedia app by One Key Gold and Platinum members, paid as OneKeyCash after the trip.

### Which hotel booking sites still offer a price match?

Booking.com still publishes a price match with its own conditions, and many hotel chains offer best rate guarantees for direct bookings. Read the current terms before you rely on any of them.

# How hotel dynamic pricing works

Every hotel price you see is the output of a system weighing demand, channels and markets in real time. Knowing how it works helps you book at a better price.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/how-hotel-dynamic-pricing-works.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: Hidden prices

## Key takeaways

- Hotels use yield management because an empty room tonight earns nothing and cannot be sold again later.
- Revenue management systems raise prices when bookings run ahead of forecast and lower them when bookings lag.
- OTA commissions differ by channel and market, which is one reason the same hotel shows different prices on different sites.
- Different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions, so the same hotel is often 5-30% cheaper from another country.
- A hotel price is a snapshot: book refundable, keep checking, and search from other countries before you pay.

Every time you search for a hotel, the price you see is the output of a pricing system that weighs many variables in real time. Knowing how that system works helps you book at a better price, and it explains why two people looking at the same hotel on the same night can see different numbers.

## The basics of yield management

A hotel has a fixed number of rooms and a product that expires every night. A room left empty tonight earns nothing, and that revenue cannot be recovered later. This constraint drives hotels to use yield management: adjusting prices across all dates to maximize total revenue.

Revenue management systems (RMS) forecast demand for each future date from historical booking patterns, the current pace of bookings, local events, day-of-week trends and seasonality. If bookings for a date run ahead of forecast, the system raises prices. If they lag, it lowers prices to stimulate demand.

> Chart: Illustrative: revenue management moves the price of the same stay as arrival approaches.

## The signals a revenue management system watches

An RMS does not look at one number. It combines many inputs into a recommended price for each date and room type:

- **Booking pace.** How quickly a date is filling compared with the same date in past years.

- **Occupancy forecast.** How full the hotel is expected to be on the night.

- **Competitor prices.** What similar hotels nearby are charging for the same dates.

- **Events and calendars.** Conferences, concerts, sports events and public holidays.

- **Length of stay.** A hotel may price a one-night stay differently from a stay that fills a gap in its calendar.

- **Cancellations and group releases.** Rooms coming back into inventory can push prices down.

## Demand-based price adjustments

The most visible form of dynamic pricing is demand-based. A city hotel that charges $180 a night on a quiet Tuesday in November may charge $380 on a Saturday during a major conference. The room is the same on both nights, and the difference comes from demand.

RMS platforms such as Duetto, IDeaS and Atomize process booking data continuously. They look at confirmed bookings and also at search activity, shopping data from travel sites and competitor prices. A surge in searches for hotels in a city, for example after a concert or sports event is announced, can lead to higher prices within hours, before many bookings have been made.

Demand also works in your favor. When a date fills slower than expected, the same system lowers the price, sometimes after you have already booked. That is why a refundable booking is worth more than it looks. See [why hotel prices change daily](https://arbitrica.com/blog/why-do-hotel-prices-change-daily.html) for more on day-to-day movement.

## OTA commission structures

Online travel agencies (OTAs) charge hotels a commission on each booking, which industry guides commonly put in the range of 15-25% of the rate. Commissions vary by market, by platform and by the hotel's negotiating power. A large chain may pay a lower percentage than an independent boutique hotel.

These differences affect the prices you see. A hotel may offer a lower rate on a channel where it pays less commission, or adjust its base rate to protect its margin across channels. That is one reason the same hotel on the same night can show different prices on different sites.

## Country-specific rates and channels

On top of demand and commissions sits a layer many travelers never see: the country you search from. Hotels sell through many channels, including global OTAs, regional booking sites, wholesalers and local partners. Different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions.

As a result, searching the same hotel from another country can open up prices you cannot get from your own country. A Barcelona hotel might be $220 a night when searched from the United States and noticeably less when searched from another country, through a local channel or a market-specific promotion. Both prices can be available at the same time.

> Chart: In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler’s own country. The typical gap was 20–40%.

In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler's own country, with a typical gap of 20-40%. The same hotel is often 5-30% cheaper from somewhere else, a spread that can be larger than the day-to-day swings caused by demand. The guide to [hidden hotel prices](https://arbitrica.com/blog/hidden-hotel-prices-guide.html) explains where these offers come from.

## Currency, taxes and fees

Prices also vary with display currency and with how taxes and fees are shown. Some markets display tax-inclusive prices, others add taxes at the end. Rates in local currency are often rounded to familiar price points. A lower headline price is only lower if it covers the identical hotel with all taxes and fees included.

## Common myths about hotel dynamic pricing

- **"Prices only go up as the date gets closer."** On high-demand dates they often do, but when a date fills slowly the system lowers the price, sometimes in the last days before arrival.

- **"There is a magic day of the week to book."** Prices respond to demand for each stay date, not to the weekday you happen to search on. When you stay usually matters more than when you book.

- **"Clearing cookies resets the price."** Cookies and private windows do not change the inventory, channels or local rates available to the country you search from.

- **"The headline price is the price."** The final total, with taxes, fees and currency conversion, is the only number worth comparing.

## What this means for travelers

The price you see reflects when you search, which channel you use and which country you search from. Two practical conclusions follow. First, a price is a snapshot: it can drop after you book, and free cancellation lets you take advantage of that. Second, the price from your own country is one of many prices for the same hotel.

- **Book a refundable rate**It lets you benefit if the system lowers the price later.

- **Watch the total, not the nightly rate**Taxes, resort fees and currency conversion change the real price.

- **Check flexible dates**Moving a stay by a night can avoid an event or a weekend peak.

- **Search from other countries**The same hotel can be priced lower in another market at the same moment.

- **Keep checking until free cancellation ends**Rebook if the identical hotel gets cheaper, and cancel only after the new booking is confirmed.

## How Arbitrica works with dynamic pricing

Searching all 195 countries by hand, one VPN connection at a time, is impossible in practice. Arbitrica, a personal AI agent that lives in your browser, does it at checkout: it searches the same hotel from 195 countries, finds the lowest price on Earth for it at a different provider than the one you are on, validates that the price is for the identical hotel with all taxes and fees included, and prepares the booking so you only review and pay.

> Chart: Geographic arbitrage (other countries, at checkout) and time arbitrage (later moments, after you pay).

Its approach also repeats the search after you book, until the free-cancellation window ends, and prepares a re-booking if the price falls, with the new booking confirmed before the original is cancelled. Research showed that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking with Arbitrica, and up to $3,000 a year. The [how it works](https://arbitrica.com/how-it-works.html) page shows the full flow.

Dynamic pricing is not limited to hotels. Flights, event tickets, online retail and subscriptions use similar systems, and the same mechanisms, searching from other countries and searching again over time, apply to them too.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is hotel dynamic pricing?

It is the practice of changing hotel prices continuously based on demand, booking pace, competitor prices, events and other signals, usually through a revenue management system.

### Why does the same hotel cost different amounts on different sites?

Hotels pay different commissions on different channels and markets, and they sell through different partners in different countries. Each channel and market can end up with a different price.

### Do hotel prices go down as well as up?

Yes. When a date fills slower than forecast, the system lowers prices to stimulate demand, which is why a refundable booking can be rebooked lower.

### Does the country I search from affect the hotel price?

It can. Different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions, so searching the same hotel from another country can open up lower prices.

# How to find the cheapest hotel rates online

A step-by-step method for the lowest hotel price: what to compare, when to book, and why the country you search from matters.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/how-to-find-cheapest-hotel-rates-online.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: Hidden prices

## Key takeaways

- The same hotel on the same dates has many prices at once, across sites, rate types, moments and countries.
- Always compare the full checkout total for the identical room type, board basis and cancellation terms.
- Book a refundable rate early, keep checking until free cancellation ends, and confirm any new booking before cancelling the old one.
- In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler's own, with a typical gap of 20-40%.
- Arbitrica searches the same hotel from 195 countries at checkout and prepares everything at the lowest price on Earth for you to review and pay.

Finding the cheapest hotel rate online is less about one secret website and more about method. The same hotel, on the same dates, can carry many prices at once: different sites, different rate types, different moments and different countries all produce a different number. This guide pulls together everything that reliably lowers what you pay, in the order that makes the biggest difference, with links to deeper guides on each step.

## Why one hotel has many prices

Hotels sell the same stay through many channels: their own website, large online travel agencies, wholesalers, tour operators, corporate programs and loyalty schemes. Each channel can have its own rates, promotions and terms. On top of that, a revenue management system adjusts prices as demand, occupancy and competitor rates change, often several times a day. Our explainer on [how hotel dynamic pricing works](https://arbitrica.com/blog/how-hotel-dynamic-pricing-works.html) covers this in detail.

The practical effect is simple. There is no single "real" price for a hotel. There is a range, and the lowest hotel price in that range goes to people who look in the right places at the right time. Many of those prices never show up in a normal search, which is what people mean by [hidden hotel prices](https://arbitrica.com/blog/hidden-hotel-prices-guide.html).

## Step one: compare the full price, not the nightly rate

Before anything else, decide what you are comparing. A low nightly rate can turn into a high total once city taxes, resort fees, cleaning charges and payment fees are added. Some sites show prices before tax, others include it, and some add mandatory fees only on the final screen.

- Use the final checkout total for the whole stay, in your currency.

- Check that each offer is for the same room type, board basis (room only, breakfast) and number of guests.

- Check the cancellation terms. A non-refundable rate is a different product from a flexible one.

Every other technique in this guide only works if you are comparing like for like.

TipTake a screenshot or note of the full total for your first offer, including fees and the cancellation deadline. That is your benchmark for everything else you find.

## Step two: check more than one site, including the hotel's own

Large booking sites, metasearch engines and the hotel's own website frequently show different prices for the same stay. Hotels often offer member rates on their own sites, and large agencies run their own loyalty programs, such as Booking.com's Genius program and Expedia Group's One Key, which can unlock lower rates for signed-in members. Joining usually only takes an email address, and it is worth signing in before you compare.

Be aware of what each source is. A metasearch result is a list of offers from other sites. A wholesale or package rate may come with conditions, such as being sold only with a flight. Read the terms before assuming a lower number is the same deal.

## Step three: choose the right time to book, and keep checking

Timing matters in two ways: when you stay and when you book. Business hotels are often cheaper at weekends, leisure hotels often cheaper midweek, and event dates are more expensive whenever you book. The guide to [the best time to book hotels](https://arbitrica.com/blog/best-time-to-book-hotels.html) sets out booking windows by type of trip.

The most useful timing habit is to book a refundable rate early and keep checking until free cancellation ends. Prices move both ways after you book. If the identical hotel gets cheaper, book again at the lower total and cancel the first booking, always in that order, so you are never without a reservation. This is time arbitrage, and [how to rebook a hotel at a lower price](https://arbitrica.com/blog/rebook-hotel-at-lower-price.html) walks through it step by step.

> Chart: Illustrative: the price of the same hotel keeps moving after you book. A drop before free cancellation ends can be rebooked.

## Step four: search from other countries

This is the step most travelers skip, and it is often the largest saving. Different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions. Searching the same hotel from another country can open up lower prices you cannot get from your own country.

In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler's own country, and the typical gap was 20-40%. Independent research points the same way: a 2024 NordVPN study found that travel bookings made through US websites came out up to 70% higher than through websites elsewhere (its largest gap was a car rental). One a seven-night stay in a triple room at a Milan hotel for a family of three cost about $1,216 searched from the US and $1,012 searched from Italy.

> Chart: In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler’s own country. The typical gap was 20–40%.

Which country is best depends on the hotel and the dates, so there is no permanent winner. Our analysis of the [cheapest country to book hotels from](https://arbitrica.com/blog/cheapest-country-to-book-hotels-from.html) explains which patterns tend to repeat and why.

### Doing it with a VPN

The manual way to search from another country is a VPN. Connect to a country, clear cookies or open a private window, search the hotel, write down the full total, and repeat. It works, but it is slow: each country takes minutes, you have to guess which countries to try, and you still have to check the payment currency, card fees and terms on each offer. Most people manage a handful of countries before giving up. [VPN vs Arbitrica for hotel booking](https://arbitrica.com/blog/vpn-vs-arbitrica-hotel-booking.html) sets the two approaches side by side.

## Step five: check the payment details

A lower rate found from another country may be charged in a foreign currency. Check whether your card adds a foreign transaction fee and whether the site offers to convert the price for you at its own exchange rate, which is often worse than your card's. Paying in the local currency with a card that has no foreign transaction fee usually gives the best result. Confirm whether you pay now or at the hotel, because a pay-at-hotel rate is charged at the exchange rate on the day you pay.

## A quick reference: what each technique is worth

| Technique | Effort | What it catches |

| Comparing full totals | Low | Fees and taxes that make a low rate expensive. |

| Checking several sites and member rates | Low to medium | Channel and loyalty differences for the same stay. |

| Flexible dates | Low | Weekday and weekend patterns, event weeks. |

| Refundable booking, then rebooking | Medium, ongoing | Price drops after you book. |

| Searching from other countries | High by hand | Country-specific inventory, local rates and promotions. |

## How Arbitrica finds the lowest hotel price for you

The two techniques with the biggest payoff, searching from other countries and repricing after you book, are also the ones that take the most time. Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that does both.

When you reach checkout for a hotel, Arbitrica searches the same hotel from 195 countries. It always looks at a different provider than the one you are on, validates that the hotel, room type, dates and terms are identical with all taxes and fees included, and checks the price will hold. It then prepares everything at the lowest price on Earth, and you review and pay.

A real example: a hotel offered at $1,527.39 on Booking.com was found by Arbitrica for $1,180.27 for the identical hotel, earning the user $347.12 (23%). Research demonstrated that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking, and up to $3,000 a year.

> Chart: A real booking: offered at $1,527.39, found for $1,180.27 for the identical hotel. Arbitrica earned the user $347.12 (23%).

After you book a refundable rate, Arbitrica's approach repeats the search until free cancellation ends. If the identical hotel becomes available at a lower price, a new booking is prepared and confirmed first, and only then is the original cancelled. ## The complete method in five steps

- **Set your benchmark**Note the full checkout total, room type and cancellation deadline of the first offer you like.

- **Check several sites and sign in**Compare the same stay on large booking sites and the hotel's own site, with member rates unlocked.

- **Book a refundable rate**Secure the hotel early while keeping the option to change it.

- **Search from other countries**By hand with a VPN for a few countries, or let an agent search from 195 countries at checkout.

- **Keep checking until free cancellation ends**Rebook when the identical hotel gets cheaper, and cancel only after the new booking is confirmed.

Follow this method and you will rarely overpay, whatever tools you use. The cheapest hotel rate online is almost never the first one you see. It is the lowest full total for the identical hotel, found by looking across sites, across time and from other countries.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the best way to find the cheapest hotel rate online?

Compare the full total on several sites with member rates unlocked, book a refundable rate, keep checking until free cancellation ends, and search the same hotel from other countries.

### Is booking directly with the hotel cheaper?

Sometimes, especially with member rates on the hotel's own site, but not always. Compare the full total and terms against large booking sites before deciding.

### Why do hotel prices differ by country?

Different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions, so searching the same hotel from another country can open up lower prices.

### Can I get a lower price after booking a hotel?

Yes, if your rate has free cancellation. Book the identical hotel again at the lower total, make sure the new booking is confirmed, then cancel the original before the deadline.

# How to save money on hotels in 2026

Seven tactics ranked by how much they move the price, from searching the same hotel in other countries to rebooking after a drop.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/how-to-save-money-on-hotels.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: Save money

## Key takeaways

- The biggest lever is geographic arbitrage: the same hotel is often 5-30% cheaper when searched from another country.
- A rate with free cancellation lets you rebook if the price drops later, which usually outweighs its small premium.
- Keep searching after you book and rebook the identical hotel if it gets cheaper, confirming the new booking before cancelling.
- Compare the final amount charged in your own currency, including card and conversion fees.
- Research showed that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking with Arbitrica, and up to $3,000 a year.

Most hotel savings advice is a list of small tricks. A few of them help, but one tactic moves the price far more than the rest: searching the same hotel from other countries before you pay. Below are seven tactics that save money on hotels in 2026, ranked by impact, with what each one is worth and how much effort it takes.

Short versionSearch the same hotel from other countries before you pay, book a rate with free cancellation, keep searching after you book, check the hotel's own site, book at a sensible time, count currency and card fees, and let an agent do the repetitive part. The biggest lever is the first one: geographic arbitrage, searching the same hotel from other countries.

## What is the single biggest way to save money on hotels in 2026?

Geographic arbitrage. Different countries get access to different inventory, sales channels, local rates and promotions, so searching the same hotel from another country can open up lower prices you cannot get from your own country. The same hotel is often 5-30% cheaper when you search from somewhere else. No other tactic on this list moves the price as much.

> Chart: In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler’s own country. The typical gap was 20–40%.

In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler's own country, and the typical gap was 20-40%.

## Why do hotel prices differ from one country to another?

Hotels sell through many channels at once: online travel agencies, wholesalers, local partners and their own sites. Each country gets its own mix of those channels, plus local rates and promotions aimed at that market. The result is that the identical hotel, on the identical night, can have a different best price depending on which country you search from.

For more detail, see our [explainer on why Booking.com prices differ by country](https://arbitrica.com/blog/booking-com-different-prices-vpn-explained.html) and the guide to [geographic price arbitrage](https://arbitrica.com/blog/what-is-geographic-price-arbitrage.html).

## The seven tactics that actually save money on hotels

### 1. Search the same hotel from other countries

Check the same hotel, on the same dates, from as many countries as you can, and book the lowest price that includes all taxes and fees. By hand this means a VPN and one country at a time, which works for a handful of countries and is impossible in practice for all 195. Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that does this at checkout: it searches the same hotel from 195 countries, validates that the lower price is for the identical hotel with all taxes and fees included, and prepares the booking so you only review and pay.

### 2. Choose rates with free cancellation

Non-refundable rates are usually a little lower at booking, but they lock you in. A rate with free cancellation lets you act if the price drops later, which is what tactic 3 depends on. One later drop is often enough to cover the small premium you paid for flexibility.

### 3. Keep searching after you book

Hotel prices keep moving after you book. If your reservation is refundable, you can book the identical hotel again when a lower price appears and then cancel the original, as long as you are still inside the free-cancellation window. This is time arbitrage. Arbitrica's approach, multiple-time arbitrage, repeats the search from 195 countries after you book until the free-cancellation window ends, then prepares a new booking at the lower price. The new booking is confirmed before the original is cancelled. Post-booking trackers such as Pruvo and RoomHawk alert you to a lower price and leave the rebooking to you.

> Chart: Multiple-time arbitrage: the search repeats after a refundable booking. The new booking is confirmed first; only then is the original cancelled.

### 4. Check the hotel's own site

Major chains (Marriott, Hilton, IHG, Hyatt, Accor) sometimes offer member rates below the online travel agency price, often with perks like breakfast or late checkout. If you belong to a loyalty program, check both. Arbitrica looks for the lowest price on Earth at a different provider than the one you are booking on, and the provider itself is never the point: the identical hotel at the lowest total is.

### 5. Book at a sensible time

Booking many months ahead rarely gets the lowest price, and waiting for the last few days before check-in is a gamble. For most trips, a few weeks to a couple of months out is a reasonable default, and earlier for peak season and major events. Because a booking with free cancellation can be replaced, booking early and then searching again is usually safer than waiting. The guide to the [best time to book hotels](https://arbitrica.com/blog/best-time-to-book-hotels.html) goes into booking windows and days of the week.

### 6. Count currency and card fees

A price shown in another currency can look lower and then lose a few percent to your card's foreign transaction fee, or to a currency conversion offered at checkout. Compare the final amount you will be charged in your own currency. Cards without foreign transaction fees, such as Capital One Venture X and Chase Sapphire Preferred, and multi-currency cards such as Wise and Revolut make this matter less. Arbitrica validates that the lower price includes all taxes and fees before it shows it to you.

### 7. Let an agent do the repetitive work

Doing tactics 1 to 6 by hand for every booking is unrealistic. Arbitrica handles the two that take the most effort: the search from 195 countries at checkout (live arbitrage) and the repeated search after you book (multiple-time arbitrage). Other trackers (Pruvo, RoomHawk, RatePunk, Repriced, OneAir) each cover part of this. See our [2026 review of the 8 main hotel price trackers](https://arbitrica.com/blog/best-hotel-price-trackers-2026.html) for the details.

## The seven tactics at a glance

| Tactic | Impact on price | Effort by hand |

| 1. Search from other countries | Highest: often 5-30% | Very high for more than a few countries |

| 2. Free cancellation | Enables later savings | Low |

| 3. Keep searching after booking | Varies with how much the price moves | High: repeated checks until the deadline |

| 4. Hotel's own site | Sometimes lower, plus perks | Low |

| 5. Sensible booking time | Avoids peak prices | Low |

| 6. Currency and card fees | A few percent | Low |

| 7. Let an agent do it | Combines 1 and 3 | None |

## Do these tactics work beyond hotels?

Yes. The two mechanisms behind tactics 1 and 3 are not specific to hotels. Flights, car rentals, event tickets, online shopping and subscriptions are also sold through different channels and at different local prices in different countries, so searching the same item from another country can find a lower price. Anything with a cancellation or return window, such as a refundable flight, a pre-order or an order with delayed shipping, can also be bought again at a lower price before the window closes. The same mechanisms Arbitrica uses for hotels apply to these purchases.

## How much money can I realistically save on hotels?

It depends on how often you travel and where. The same hotel is often 5-30% cheaper when searched from another country. Research showed that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking with Arbitrica, and up to $3,000 a year. In one real Arbitrica search, Booking offered a hotel at $1,527.39. Arbitrica found the identical hotel for $1,180.27, earning the user $347.12 (23%).

> Chart: A real booking: offered at $1,527.39, found for $1,180.27 for the identical hotel. Arbitrica earned the user $347.12 (23%).

Arbitrica also serves companies: teams traveling to trade shows and conferences, and the operations and travel managers who book for them. For company travel, see [business travel hotel savings](https://arbitrica.com/blog/business-travel-hotel-savings.html).

## What is the cheapest way to book hotels online?

There is no single site with the lowest price. The best price depends on the hotel, the dates and which country you search from. The lowest result comes from searching the same hotel from many countries, booking a rate with free cancellation, and searching again after you book. Arbitrica does the searching from 195 countries for you and finds the lowest price on Earth for that hotel.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does it work to use a VPN to find cheaper hotels?

Sometimes, but slowly. A VPN lets you search from one country at a time. Checking a few countries by hand is possible. Checking all 195 is not practical, and that is the gap Arbitrica fills.

### What is the best day of the week to book a hotel?

The day of the week matters less than how far ahead you book and whether you can cancel. A refundable booking made at a sensible time, then searched again before the cancellation deadline, beats trying to time a specific weekday.

### Are member rates on chain hotels actually lower?

Sometimes, and they often come with perks such as breakfast or late checkout. If you are a loyalty member, check both the chain's own price and the online travel agency price.

### Is it legal to cancel and rebook a hotel for a lower rate?

Yes, provided the original reservation is refundable. Online travel agencies and chains include the cancellation right in their booking terms, so booking again at the lower rate and then cancelling the original within the free-cancellation window is allowed.

### Does Hopper or any other app do all of this?

No major app does all seven. Hopper offers products such as Price Freeze and Cancel for Any Reason on hotel bookings. Pruvo and RoomHawk alert you to price drops after booking, and RatePunk compares major booking sites, shows which country has the lowest rate and sends rebooking alerts. Arbitrica searches the same hotel from 195 countries at checkout, repeats the search after you book within the free-cancellation window, and prepares everything so you only review and pay.
