# How to save money on international hotel bookings

International stays carry the biggest hotel bills and the biggest room for savings. These are the tactics that lower the total without downgrading the hotel.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/save-money-international-hotel-bookings.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: Save money

## Key takeaways

- The same hotel is often 5-30% cheaper when searched from another country, because countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions.
- Book with free cancellation first and treat that booking as a price ceiling, not a final commitment.
- A currency conversion offered at checkout often adds a markup; compare the final amount charged in your own currency.
- Incognito mode does not change the country you search from, so it cannot open up prices from other countries.
- Arbitrica searches the same hotel from 195 countries at checkout and repeats the search after you book.

International hotel bookings carry the highest price tags and the biggest potential for savings. A week in Tokyo, Paris or Dubai can run into thousands of dollars for accommodation alone. The tactics below lower that bill without downgrading your stay, and the biggest one is searching the same hotel from other countries.

## Book with free cancellation first

Choose a rate with free cancellation whenever the hotel offers one, even if the base rate is slightly higher. The flexibility to cancel and book again at a lower price usually outweighs the small premium. Treat your first booking as a price ceiling, not a final commitment.

## Use geographic price arbitrage

Different countries get access to different inventory, sales channels, local rates and promotions. Searching the same hotel from another country can therefore open up lower prices that you cannot get from your own country. The same hotel is often 5-30% cheaper when searched from somewhere else.

> Chart: In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler’s own country. The typical gap was 20–40%.

In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler's own country, with a typical gap of 20-40%. A 2024 NordVPN study found that travel bookings made through US websites came out up to 70% higher than through websites elsewhere (its largest gap was a car rental). In its Milan example, a seven-night stay in a triple room for a family of three was about $1,216 searched from the US and $1,012 searched from Italy.

> Chart: 2024 NordVPN study: a seven-night stay in a triple room at a Milan hotel for a family of three cost about $1,216 searched from the US and $1,012 searched from Italy.

With a VPN you can check one country at a time, which makes searching all 195 impossible in practice. Arbitrica does it at checkout: it searches the same hotel from 195 countries, validates that the lower price is for the identical hotel with all taxes and fees included, and prepares the booking so you only review and pay. For the full explanation, see [what geographic price arbitrage is](https://arbitrica.com/blog/what-is-geographic-price-arbitrage.html), and for which countries tend to come out lower, the guide to the [cheapest country to book hotels from](https://arbitrica.com/blog/cheapest-country-to-book-hotels-from.html).

## Pay in the right currency

When a booking site or the hotel offers to charge you in your own currency, check the exchange rate it uses. A currency conversion offered at checkout often adds a markup over your card's own rate. Paying in the hotel's local currency with a card that has no foreign transaction fee is usually the lower-cost option. Whatever you choose, compare the final amount you will be charged, with all taxes and fees included.

## Know which taxes are paid at the hotel

Many destinations charge a city or tourist tax per person per night, and some hotels collect it at check-in rather than at booking. Resort fees and facility fees work the same way in some markets. When you compare two offers for the same hotel, check whether these charges are included in each total or listed as payable on arrival. An offer that looks lower because it leaves out a local tax is not lower.

## Check the rate conditions

Some local rates are limited to residents of a country or to holders of a local ID, and the hotel can ask for proof at check-in. Others are tied to a payment card or a membership. Read the conditions before you book and skip any rate you do not qualify for. Booking a rate that is openly offered in another market is a normal purchase.

## Search again after you book

Hotel prices keep changing between booking and check-in. If your reservation has free cancellation, a later drop is an opportunity: book the identical hotel again at the lower price, then cancel the original before the cancellation deadline. This is time arbitrage. Arbitrica's approach, multiple-time arbitrage, repeats the search from 195 countries after you book until the free-cancellation window ends, then prepares the new booking at the lower price. The new booking is confirmed before the original is cancelled.

> Chart: Multiple-time arbitrage: the search repeats after a refundable booking. The new booking is confirmed first; only then is the original cancelled.

For international stays, remember that cancellation deadlines are usually set in the hotel's local time. See [hotel price drops after booking](https://arbitrica.com/blog/hotel-price-drop-after-booking.html) for the step-by-step version.

## Don't rely on incognito mode

Searching in a private window is a popular tip. It clears cookies and your recent search history on that site, but it does not change the country you search from, so it cannot open up the prices available from other countries. Use it if you like, but do not expect it to replace the tactics above.

## Compare direct vs. OTA prices

Hotels sometimes offer lower rates on their own website to avoid paying OTA commissions. Check the hotel's site before completing an OTA booking. When the direct price is lower, you also get to deal directly with the property for any changes or issues. Arbitrica looks for the lowest price on Earth for the identical hotel at a different provider than the one you are booking on.

## Consider alternative accommodation platforms

Beyond the major OTAs, platforms like Agoda (strong in Asia), Trip.com (competitive for Asian destinations) and local booking sites often carry their own rates. A hotel listed on five platforms can have noticeably different prices on each, especially for international destinations.

## Book further in advance for peak season

During high-demand periods, hotel prices tend to rise as the date approaches. For peak season, booking two to three months out usually gives you more choice and lower prices. The free cancellation strategy still applies: book early, keep searching, and book again if the price drops. The guide to the [best time to book hotels](https://arbitrica.com/blog/best-time-to-book-hotels.html) covers booking windows in more detail.

## Use loyalty programs strategically

Hotel loyalty programs often offer member rates slightly below the public rate, plus perks such as breakfast or late checkout. Check the member rate against the best price you can find from other countries, and take whichever is lower in total.

## A checklist before you pay

- **Same hotel, same terms**Confirm the hotel, dates, guests, room type, meal plan and cancellation policy match.

- **Full total**Include taxes, resort fees and any tax payable at the hotel.

- **Your currency**Compare the amount your card will be charged, after conversion and fees.

- **Free cancellation**Prefer a rate you can cancel, so you can rebook if the price drops.

- **Other countries**Search the same hotel from other countries, or let an agent do it from 195 at checkout.

## The same approach works beyond hotels

The same two mechanisms help with the rest of an international trip. Flights, car rentals and event tickets are also sold at different local prices in different countries, and a refundable flight or car rental can be booked again at a lower price before the cancellation deadline. The same applies to online shopping and subscriptions.

## Automate the hard parts

Searching from 195 countries before you pay, and again after you book, is the part no traveler can do by hand. Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that shows up at checkout and handles both: live arbitrage when you are about to pay, and multiple-time arbitrage after you book. It finds the lowest price on Earth for the same hotel and prepares everything so you only review and pay. Research showed that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking with Arbitrica, and up to $3,000 a year. Arbitrica also serves companies: teams traveling to trade shows and conferences, and the operations and travel managers who book for them.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is it cheaper to book an international hotel from another country?

Often, yes. Different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions, and the same hotel is often 5-30% cheaper when searched from somewhere else.

### Should I pay for a foreign hotel in my own currency or the local currency?

Usually the local currency, with a card that has no foreign transaction fee. A conversion offered at checkout often adds a markup, so compare the final amount you will be charged.

### Does incognito mode get lower hotel prices abroad?

No. A private window clears cookies on that site, but it does not change the country you search from, so it cannot open up offers sold in other countries.

### What should I check before booking a local rate?

Read the rate conditions. Some local rates are limited to residents or local ID holders, and the hotel can ask for proof at check-in.

# Time arbitrage explained: how to benefit when prices drop after you buy

Many purchases can still be cancelled or returned after you pay. Inside that window, a price drop is money you can still get.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/time-arbitrage-explained.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: Save money

## Key takeaways

- Time arbitrage means getting the same item at a lower price by searching for it at more than one point in time.
- Live arbitrage happens at checkout; multiple-time arbitrage repeats the search after purchase until the cancellation or return window ends.
- Hotels with free cancellation, pay-later car rentals, flexible flights, pre-orders and online orders with a return window suit it best.
- Always secure the new booking or purchase first, then cancel or return the original.
- Combined with geographic arbitrage, every search becomes a grid of many countries at many points in time.

You book a hotel, order a pre-release console or buy concert tickets, and a week later the same thing is cheaper. Most people shrug and move on. But a lot of purchases come with a window in which you can still cancel, return or change them, and inside that window a price drop after purchase is money you can still get.

Time arbitrage is the name for doing that on purpose. This guide explains what it is, where it works, where it does not, and how it combines with geographic arbitrage.

## What is time arbitrage?

Time arbitrage means getting the same item at a lower price by searching for it at more than one point in time. It works because prices for hotels, flights, tickets and many products change constantly, and because many purchases can be undone for a period after you pay.

> Chart: Illustrative: the price of the same hotel keeps moving after you book. A drop before free cancellation ends can be rebooked.

There are two forms:

- **Live arbitrage** happens at checkout, in real time. Right before you pay, the same item is searched again so you buy at the lowest price that exists at that moment.

- **Multiple-time arbitrage** happens after you buy. The search is repeated at many points in time until the cancellation or return window ends. If the identical item becomes cheaper, a new purchase is prepared at the lower price, and the original is cancelled or returned only once the new one is confirmed.

|  | Live arbitrage | Multiple-time arbitrage |

| When it runs | At checkout, before you pay | After purchase, until the cancellation or return window ends |

| What it catches | A lower price available right now | Price drops that appear later |

| What it needs | A search at the moment of purchase | A purchase you can cancel or return, and repeated searches |

| Result | You pay less from the start | You rebook or repurchase at the lower price |

## Where price drops after purchase happen

### Hotels

Hotels are the clearest case. Prices are set night by night and move with demand, competitor prices and cancellations, as we explain in [why hotel prices change daily](https://arbitrica.com/blog/why-do-hotel-prices-change-daily.html). Many rates come with free cancellation until a day or a few days before arrival. If the same hotel, dates and rate type get cheaper before that deadline, you can book the new price and cancel the old one. Our article on [hotel price drops after booking](https://arbitrica.com/blog/hotel-price-drop-after-booking.html) goes through it step by step.

### Flights

Airfares change as seats in each fare class sell. In the United States, Department of Transportation rules require airlines to let you either hold a reservation or cancel it without penalty within 24 hours of booking, when you book at least seven days before departure. Beyond that window, it depends on the ticket. Flexible fares can often be changed, and some airlines give credit for the difference when the fare drops. Basic fares usually allow very little.

### Car rentals

Pay-later car rental reservations can usually be cancelled without a fee, and rental prices move a lot with demand around holidays and events. That makes them a good fit for repeated searches until pickup.

### Event tickets

Ticket prices are increasingly dynamic. The 2024 Oasis reunion sale in the UK drew wide complaints when prices rose during the queue, and the Competition and Markets Authority opened an investigation into it. Prices can also fall, especially on resale platforms as an event gets closer and sellers compete. Time arbitrage only helps here when the purchase can be refunded, exchanged or resold, so the terms of the specific ticket matter more than for hotels. Read more in [event ticket price drops](https://arbitrica.com/blog/event-ticket-price-drops.html).

### Pre-orders and delayed-shipment e-commerce

Online orders often have a gap between purchase and delivery, and prices keep moving in that gap. Amazon.com runs a pre-order price guarantee on eligible items: if its price falls between your order and the end of the release day, you pay the lowest price. For orders that are not covered, you can often cancel before the item ships and reorder at the new price, or use the return window after delivery. In the European Union, most online purchases of goods come with a 14-day right of withdrawal, which creates a similar window. The guide to [Amazon prices in different countries](https://arbitrica.com/blog/amazon-prices-different-countries.html) covers the shopping side.

### Subscriptions

Annual plans for software, streaming and other services change price with promotions, and they often cost different amounts in different countries. When a service lets you cancel and get a refund for a short period after an annual purchase, a lower price for the same plan during that period can be used in the same way.

## How time arbitrage combines with geographic arbitrage

Time arbitrage asks *when* the price is lowest. Geographic arbitrage asks *where*. The same hotel or product can have a different price when bought from another country, because different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions. See [what geographic price arbitrage is](https://arbitrica.com/blog/what-is-geographic-price-arbitrage.html) for the details.

> Chart: Geographic arbitrage (other countries, at checkout) and time arbitrage (later moments, after you pay).

Put the two together and every search becomes a grid: many countries at many points in time. A single search from your own country checks one cell of that grid. The lowest price is often in a cell nobody would think to check by hand, such as an unexpected country three days after you booked.

Arbitrica is built on this combination:

- **Search from 195 countries at checkout**It searches the same item from 195 countries and finds the lowest price on Earth for it at a different provider than the one you are on. That is live arbitrage plus geographic arbitrage.

- **Validate**It checks that the lower price is for the identical item, with all taxes and fees included, and that the price will not suddenly change.

- **Prepare**It prepares the purchase so you only review and pay.

- **Repeat after purchase**Arbitrica's approach repeats the search from 195 countries until the cancellation or return window ends. When it finds a lower price, it prepares the new booking or purchase at that price, and the new one is confirmed before the original is cancelled. That is multiple-time arbitrage.

In one real hotel booking, the stay was offered on Booking for $1,527.39. Arbitrica found the identical hotel for $1,180.27, earning the user $347.12, about 23 percent. Research showed that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking and up to $3,000 a year with Arbitrica, $34 per online purchase and up to $3,000 a year, and $107 per event ticket purchase and up to $1,500 a year. You can see the full flow on [how it works](https://arbitrica.com/how-it-works.html).

> Chart: Research demonstrated average earnings of $47 per hotel booking, $34 per online purchase and $107 per event ticket purchase, and up to $3,000, $3,000 and $1,500 a year.

## What to watch before you rebook or repurchase

Time arbitrage only pays when the new deal is truly the same and truly cheaper. Check these before you act:

- **Identical item.** Same hotel, dates, guests, rate type and meal plan. For products, same model, condition and seller warranty.

- **Final total.** Taxes, resort fees, booking fees, shipping and currency conversion all count.

- **Cancellation or return costs.** Cancellation fees, restocking fees and return shipping can wipe out a small saving.

- **Deadlines.** Hotel cancellation deadlines are often set in the hotel's local time. Return windows usually start on delivery, not purchase.

- **Order of steps.** Secure the new booking first, then cancel the original, so you are never left without one.

- **Refund timing.** Your card may show both charges for a few days until the refund clears.

## Can you do time arbitrage by hand?

Yes, within limits. Book flexible rates, put the cancellation deadline in your calendar and check the same item every few days. Price history sites such as camelcamelcamel help for Amazon products, and airline and booking sites offer price alerts. The limit is effort: each check covers one moment from one country, and most people stop after a couple of tries. That is the gap an automated approach fills.

Companies face the same problem at scale. Travel managers and operations managers with dozens of refundable bookings open at once rarely have time to check each one again before its deadline, and Arbitrica also serves companies for exactly that reason.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is time arbitrage?

Time arbitrage means getting the same item at a lower price by searching for it at more than one point in time, either at checkout (live arbitrage) or repeatedly after purchase while it can still be cancelled or returned (multiple-time arbitrage).

### What can I do if the price drops after purchase?

If your purchase can be cancelled or returned, buy the identical item at the lower price first, then cancel or return the original before the deadline. Check fees and the final total so the saving is real.

### Which purchases work best for time arbitrage?

Hotels with free cancellation, pay-later car rentals, flexible flights, pre-orders and online orders with a return window. Event tickets and subscriptions work only when the specific terms allow a refund, exchange or resale.

### How does time arbitrage relate to geographic arbitrage?

Geographic arbitrage finds the lowest price for the same item from different countries. Time arbitrage repeats that search at different points in time. Combined, they check many countries at many moments.

# Trade show hotel prices: why they spike and how teams pay less

Compression, room blocks and strict terms push show-week prices far above normal. Here is how exhibitor teams pay less for the same hotels.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/trade-show-hotel-prices.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: For companies

## Key takeaways

- Trade show hotel prices spike because of compression: citywide demand runs well ahead of hotel supply during show week.
- Official room blocks give a fixed rate and protection from peaks, but they are not always the lowest price for the same hotel.
- Minimum stays, deposits and early cancellation deadlines can raise the real cost of a show-week booking well above the nightly rate.
- Book refundable rates early, then search the same hotel again before the deadline and from other countries.
- Arbitrica serves companies too: it searches the same hotel from 195 countries at checkout and confirms any rebooking before the original is cancelled.

If your company exhibits at a major trade show, you already know the pattern. A hotel that sells at a normal business rate most of the year can cost several times that during show week, usually with a minimum stay and a deposit attached. For a team of booth staff, a setup crew and a couple of executives, hotels quickly become one of the largest lines in the show budget.

This guide explains why trade show hotel prices behave this way, what that means for conference hotel rates and exhibition hotel costs, and what teams can do to pay less for the same hotels.

## Why hotel prices spike around trade shows

Three forces work together during a big show: compression, hotel blocks and stricter booking terms.

### Compression

Compression is the hotel industry's word for demand that runs well ahead of supply. When tens of thousands of exhibitors and visitors arrive in one city for the same few days, hotels near the venue fill early. Revenue management systems watch the pace of bookings and raise prices as forecast occupancy climbs. Once the hotels closest to the venue fill, demand spills outward, and hotels across the city and in neighboring towns raise their prices too.

> Chart: Illustrative: revenue management moves the price of the same stay as arrival approaches.

Prices around a show do not only go up. A hotel that priced high three months out may lower its price if bookings come in slower than forecast, or when unsold group inventory is released back for sale. That movement is what makes re-searching worthwhile, as covered below.

### Hotel blocks and official housing

Most large shows contract inventory at partner hotels in advance and sell it through an official housing provider. The industry calls this a room block. Block rates are fixed in the contract, which protects attendees from the worst peaks, but they are not always the lowest price available for the same hotel. Blocks also have a cut-off date, after which unsold inventory goes back to the hotel and the block rate may no longer apply.

Organizers usually sign attrition clauses: if their block goes unused, they may owe the hotel a penalty. Some shows pass that pressure on by tying exhibitor benefits, such as housing priority or booth placement points, to booking inside the official block. Read the exhibitor manual before booking elsewhere so you know what, if anything, you give up.

### Minimum stays, deposits and strict cancellation

During peak events many hotels require a minimum length of stay that covers the core show days, even if your team only needs two nights. Deposits or full prepayment at booking are common, and cancellation deadlines move from the usual day or two before arrival to weeks before. A price that looks reasonable per night can cost much more once the forced extra nights and the stricter terms are counted.

| Driver | What happens | Effect on your bill |

| Compression | Citywide demand outruns supply, and hotels raise prices as occupancy forecasts rise | Higher nightly prices, also at hotels far from the venue |

| Hotel blocks | Inventory contracted in advance at fixed rates, released at the cut-off date | Predictable price inside the block, but not always the lowest |

| Minimum stays | Hotels require a set number of nights over the show dates | You pay for nights the team does not need |

| Deposits and prepayment | Payment taken at booking or weeks before arrival | Cash tied up early and less flexibility |

| Strict cancellation | Deadlines set weeks before arrival | Changes to the team list become expensive |

## Why exhibitor teams pay more than they need to

Trade show travel rarely gets booked in one go. The setup crew needs nights before the show opens. Booth staff are confirmed in waves. Executives decide late. Each person, or an assistant, books whatever looks acceptable at that moment, usually from one website and always from one country. Nobody goes back to check the same hotel a month later, because everyone has moved on to the next task.

The result is a mix of early bookings at prices that may have dropped since, late bookings at peak prices, and non-refundable rates that cannot be changed when the team list changes. For a wider view of company hotel costs, see the guide to [business travel hotel savings](https://arbitrica.com/blog/business-travel-hotel-savings.html).

## How teams can cut trade show hotel prices

- **Book refundable, and book early.**As soon as show dates and a rough headcount are known, reserve refundable rates at the hotels you want. Early bookings secure availability, and free cancellation keeps the option to switch. For a peak week, a refundable rate that costs a little more per night is usually worth it.

- **Compare the block rate with the open market.**Check the same hotel and dates outside the official housing channel. If the open price is lower and the exhibitor manual does not penalize booking outside the block, book where the price is lower.

- **Re-search the same hotel later.**Prices move as the show approaches, hotels release unsold group inventory and forecasts change. Search the identical hotel, dates and rate type again every week or two until the cancellation deadline. If it is cheaper, make the new booking first, confirm it, and only then cancel the original. Our article on [time arbitrage](https://arbitrica.com/blog/time-arbitrage-explained.html) explains why this works.

- **Search from other countries.**Different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions, so the same hotel can cost less when searched from another country. This is [geographic price arbitrage](https://arbitrica.com/blog/what-is-geographic-price-arbitrage.html), and the spread for the same hotel is often 5-30%.

- **Adjust dates and distance where you can.**Setup crews arrive before the peak and can sometimes stay a little farther out on those nights, then move closer for show days. A hotel a few transit stops away can be far less affected by compression.

- **Keep one booking log.**Track every traveler's hotel, confirmation number, price, rate type and cancellation deadline in the hotel's local time. Without it, re-searching and cancelling on time does not happen.

- **Ignore unsolicited housing offers.**Exhibitors at large shows are often contacted by companies that imply they are the official housing provider, and organizers warn about them regularly. Book through the official channel, directly with a hotel or through a booking site you know.

> Chart: In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler’s own country. The typical gap was 20–40%.

In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler's own country, with a typical gap of 20-40%. During show week, when nightly prices are at their highest, a gap of that size is worth more in dollars than at any other time of year.

## Conference hotel rates: comparing your options

Each way of booking show week has a different trade-off. The aim is the same hotel at the lowest final price, with terms that fit a team list that will change.

| Option | Strengths | Watch out for |

| Official hotel block | Fixed rate, show-related benefits, protection from peak prices | Cut-off dates, attrition pressure, not always the lowest price |

| Booking with the hotel directly | Direct relationship, loyalty points | Minimum stays and deposits during show week |

| Online booking sites | Wide choice, many refundable rates | Prices change daily, and non-refundable rates look tempting |

| The same hotel searched from other countries | Access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions | You must confirm it is the identical hotel with all taxes and fees |

## How Arbitrica fits trade show travel

Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that shows up at the checkout when you are about to pay for a hotel. It works for individual travelers and for companies, including teams heading to trade shows and conferences. For each booking, it does the steps above that cannot be done by hand at scale:

- It searches the same hotel from 195 countries and finds the lowest price on Earth for it at a different provider than the one you are on.

- It validates that the lower price is for the identical hotel and includes all taxes and fees, and checks that the price will not suddenly change.

- It automatically prepares everything, so the traveler, or the person booking for the team, only reviews and pays.

- After booking, Arbitrica's approach repeats the search at multiple points in time until the free cancellation window ends. When the identical hotel gets cheaper, it prepares a new booking at the lower price. The new booking is confirmed before the original is cancelled.

> Chart: Multiple-time arbitrage: the search repeats after a refundable booking. The new booking is confirmed first; only then is the original cancelled.

Research showed that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking and up to $3,000 a year. In one real booking, a hotel was offered on Booking for $1,527.39. Arbitrica found the identical hotel for $1,180.27 and earned the user $347.12, about 23%. During show week, when nightly prices are at their highest, the same percentage spread is worth more in dollars.

The same mechanisms apply beyond hotels, including flights, car rentals and event tickets. See [how it works](https://arbitrica.com/how-it-works.html) for the full flow, and [cutting business travel costs for operations managers](https://arbitrica.com/blog/operations-manager-travel-costs.html) for crew travel outside show season.

## Frequently asked questions

### Why are hotel prices so high during trade shows?

Large shows create compression: citywide demand runs well ahead of hotel supply, so revenue management systems raise prices as occupancy forecasts climb. Minimum stays, deposits and strict cancellation terms add to the total.

### Is the official hotel block always the cheapest option?

No. Block rates are fixed in advance and protect against the worst peaks, but the same hotel can be priced lower on the open market or when searched from another country. Check the exhibitor manual for any benefits tied to booking inside the block.

### When should we book hotels for a trade show?

As soon as show dates and a rough headcount are known. Book refundable rates early to secure availability, then search the same hotel again before the cancellation deadline in case the price drops.

### Can we rebook if the hotel gets cheaper after we book?

Yes, if the original booking has free cancellation. Book the identical hotel, dates and rate type at the lower price first, confirm it, and then cancel the original before the deadline.

### How does Arbitrica help companies with trade show hotel costs?

Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that searches the same hotel from 195 countries at checkout, validates the identical hotel with all taxes and fees, and prepares the booking. After booking, its approach repeats the search until the free cancellation window ends, and the new booking is confirmed before the original is cancelled.

# How to reduce corporate hotel spend: a travel manager's guide

Negotiated programs help, but they leave gaps. Here is where corporate hotel spend leaks and how to close it without moving travelers to worse hotels.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/travel-manager-hotel-savings.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: For companies

## Key takeaways

- Rate leakage has two forms: bookings made outside the company channel, and in-channel bookings at a higher rate than the one negotiated.
- Static negotiated rates protect against peaks but can sit above public prices on quiet dates, so spot audits pay off.
- Re-shopping only works with refundable rates: match the identical booking, compare totals and confirm the new booking before cancelling.
- The same hotel is often 5-30% cheaper when searched from another country, which a single-country search never finds.
- Arbitrica serves companies as well as individuals, keeping travelers in the same hotel while finding the lowest price on Earth for it.

Hotels are one of the two largest lines in most corporate travel budgets, next to airfare, and they are harder to control. Prices change daily, the same hotel is sold through many channels, and travelers book on their own schedule. Negotiated programs help, but they leave gaps. This guide is for travel managers who want to reduce corporate hotel spend without moving travelers to worse hotels.

## Where corporate hotel spend leaks

Most hotel overspend comes from a handful of patterns. Knowing which ones apply to your program tells you where to start.

### Rate leakage

Rate leakage has two forms. The first is out-of-channel booking: travelers book outside the company's booking channel, so the negotiated rate is never applied and the nights do not count toward the volume you committed to a hotel chain. The second is in-channel leakage: the booking goes through the right channel but at a higher rate than the one negotiated, because the negotiated rate was not loaded, was not available on those dates, or the traveler picked a different rate type.

Both forms show up in your data. Match booked rates against negotiated rates for the same hotels and dates, and look for hotel nights in expense reports that have no matching booking record.

### Non-refundable rates on trips that change

Non-refundable rates are usually priced below flexible ones. Travelers pick them to look cost-conscious, then the meeting moves. One lost night can wipe out the discount from several bookings.

### Booked once, never checked again

Hotel prices keep moving after a booking is made. A traveler who booked a refundable rate three weeks out could often rebook the identical hotel for less a week later, but nobody looks.

### One country, one search

Travelers and booking channels search from your own country. The same hotel can be priced differently when searched from another country, and a single-country search never finds that price.

## Corporate hotel rates vs OTA rates

A negotiated corporate rate is a commitment from the hotel to a set price or discount, usually agreed in an annual RFP. Public rates on online travel agencies (OTAs) and hotel websites change daily. The practical question is which one is lower on the dates your travelers actually book.

| Rate type | How it is set | Strengths | Limits |

| Static negotiated rate | Fixed nightly price agreed for the year | Budget certainty, often with last room availability | Can sit above public prices on quiet dates |

| Dynamic negotiated rate | Fixed percentage off the hotel's best available rate | Follows the market down as well as up | The discount is taken from one reference price, not the lowest price available anywhere |

| Public OTA or hotel website rate | Set daily by the hotel's revenue management | Easy to find, many refundable options | No volume credit, and prices swing with demand |

| Member and mobile rates | Discounts for logged-in or app users | Sometimes below corporate rates | Conditions vary, and a loyalty account may be needed |

| The same hotel searched from another country | Different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions | Often 5-30% below the price from your own country | Must be checked for identical hotel, taxes and fees |

None of these is always the lowest. Static negotiated rates protect you during peaks but can cost more than public prices on quiet dates. That is why a spot audit pays off: take a sample of last quarter's bookings and check what the same hotel cost through other channels on the same dates. Our article on [business travel hotel savings](https://arbitrica.com/blog/business-travel-hotel-savings.html) works through an example.

## Refundable rates and re-shopping

Re-shopping means checking the price of a booked hotel again before the cancellation deadline and rebooking if it has dropped. It only works with refundable rates, so the two policies belong together.

An illustrative example: a traveler books a refundable rate at $240 a night for four nights, three weeks before arrival. Ten days later the identical hotel, dates and rate type are available for $210. Rebooking saves $120 on one trip. A non-refundable rate at $225 would have looked like the better deal on the day of booking, and would have ended up costing $60 more.

> Chart: Multiple-time arbitrage: the search repeats after a refundable booking. The new booking is confirmed first; only then is the original cancelled.

Rules that keep re-shopping safe:

- Match the hotel, dates, guests, rate type, meal plan and cancellation terms exactly.

- Compare the final total with all taxes and fees included.

- Confirm the new booking before cancelling the original.

- Watch deadlines, which are often set in the hotel's local time.

- Make sure the new confirmation reaches the expense report and your duty-of-care records.

See [time arbitrage explained](https://arbitrica.com/blog/time-arbitrage-explained.html) for how the same idea applies to flights, car rentals and other bookings.

## Geographic arbitrage for corporate travel

Geographic arbitrage means buying the same item from the country where it is priced lowest. For hotels, different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions, so the identical hotel can cost less when searched from another country. The spread is often 5-30%.

> Chart: The same item, with the same dates and terms, is often 5–30% cheaper bought from another country or at another moment.

In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler's own country, with a typical gap of 20-40%. The obstacle is effort. Checking one hotel from 195 countries by hand, one VPN connection at a time, and verifying taxes and fees for each result, is impossible in practice for a single trip, let alone a whole program. Read more in [what is geographic price arbitrage](https://arbitrica.com/blog/what-is-geographic-price-arbitrage.html).

## A practical playbook for travel managers

- **Baseline your top destinations.**Pull hotel spend by city and hotel for the last 12 months. A small number of cities often accounts for most of the money.

- **Measure leakage.**Compare booked rates with negotiated rates, and expense data with booking data.

- **Make refundable the default.**Use it for trips booked more than a few days out. Allow non-refundable only when plans are firm and the discount is large.

- **Allow identical-hotel savings in policy.**If a traveler finds the same approved hotel for less, the policy should welcome it, with a clear note on how to record the booking.

- **Check volume commitments.**Find out whether nights booked outside your preferred channel still count toward targets agreed with hotel chains, and weigh that against the savings.

- **Run a pilot.**Pick a group of frequent travelers for one quarter and compare what they paid with what they would have paid.

## How Arbitrica helps travelers book the identical hotel for less

Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that serves both individual travelers and companies. It works where the money is actually spent: at the checkout, when a traveler is about to pay for a hotel.

- **At checkout:** it searches the same hotel from 195 countries and finds the lowest price on Earth for it at a different provider than the one the traveler is on.

- **Validation:** it checks that the lower price is for the identical hotel, includes all taxes and fees, and will not suddenly change.

- **Preparation:** it automatically prepares everything, so the traveler only reviews and pays.

- **After booking:** Arbitrica's approach repeats the search at multiple points in time until the free cancellation window ends, and prepares a rebooking at the lower price. The new booking is confirmed before the original is cancelled.

> Chart: At checkout Arbitrica searches the same item from 195 countries, checks it is identical with all taxes and fees included, and prepares everything at the lowest price.

Because the hotel stays the same, the traveler stays where your policy says they should. Research showed that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking and up to $3,000 a year. In one real booking, a hotel was offered on Booking for $1,527.39; Arbitrica found the identical hotel for $1,180.27 and earned the user $347.12, about 23%.

If you are weighing options built for companies, our comparison of [Arbitrica vs Pruvo](https://arbitrica.com/blog/arbitrica-vs-pruvo.html), which now focuses on business customers, covers the differences in mechanism, and the [FAQ](https://arbitrica.com/faq.html) answers common questions. For teams heading to events, see [trade show hotel prices](https://arbitrica.com/blog/trade-show-hotel-prices.html).

## Frequently asked questions

### What is rate leakage in corporate travel?

Rate leakage is hotel spend that misses the negotiated program. It happens when travelers book outside the company channel, or when bookings in the right channel end up at a higher rate than the negotiated one.

### Are corporate hotel rates always lower than OTA rates?

No. Static negotiated rates protect against peak prices but can sit above public OTA prices on quiet dates, and the same hotel can also be priced lower when searched from another country. Spot audits show where your rates stand.

### Should company policy require refundable hotel rates?

For most trips booked more than a few days ahead, yes. Refundable rates protect against changed plans and make re-shopping possible. Non-refundable rates make sense only when plans are firm and the discount is large.

### What is re-shopping a hotel booking?

Re-shopping means searching the identical hotel, dates and rate type again before the cancellation deadline. If the price has dropped, the traveler books the lower price, confirms it, and then cancels the original.

### How does Arbitrica help reduce corporate hotel spend?

Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that searches the same hotel from 195 countries at checkout, validates the identical hotel with all taxes and fees, and prepares the booking. After booking, its approach repeats the search until the free cancellation window ends, and the new booking is confirmed before the original is cancelled.

# VPN vs. Arbitrica for cheaper hotel booking

A VPN lets you check one other country at a time. Here is what that method gets right, where it runs out, and how a personal AI agent covers 195 countries instead.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/vpn-vs-arbitrica-hotel-booking.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: Comparisons

## Key takeaways

- Searching the same hotel from another country can open up lower prices, because different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions.
- A VPN checks one country per search, so in practice people test a handful of countries and miss the rest.
- At about three minutes per country, checking all 195 countries by hand would take close to ten hours for a single hotel.
- Arbitrica searches the same hotel from 195 countries at checkout, validates the identical hotel with all taxes and fees included, and prepares the booking for you to review and pay.
- A VPN is still the right choice for privacy and streaming; it is a slow way to find the lowest hotel price.

Savvy travelers have used VPNs for years to find cheaper hotel prices from other countries. The idea is simple: search the same hotel from another country and book there if the total is lower. It can work, but one country at a time is a slow way to look, and that is the problem Arbitrica was designed to solve.

## Why searching from another country can lower a hotel price

Hotels do not sell through one channel. They distribute rates through online travel agencies, wholesalers, local partners, tour operators and their own websites, and each country gets its own mix of those channels. Different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions, so searching the same hotel from another country can open up prices you cannot get from your own country.

Independent research points the same way. A 2024 NordVPN study found that travel bookings made through US websites came out up to 70% higher than through websites elsewhere (its largest gap was a car rental). In one example from that study, a seven-night stay in a triple room at a Milan hotel for a family of three cost about $1,216 searched from the US and $1,012 searched from Italy.

In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler's own country, and the typical gap was 20-40%. The catch is that the cheapest country changes from hotel to hotel and from date to date, so there is no single country you can always switch to.

> Chart: In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler’s own country. The typical gap was 20–40%.

## How the VPN approach works

You subscribe to a VPN service, connect to a server in another country (say, Thailand or Poland), and open the hotel on a booking site. If the final total is lower, you book. If not, you connect to another country and check again.

Done carefully, each check means clearing cookies or opening a private window, entering the same dates and guests again, getting all the way to the final price with taxes and fees, and noting the rate conditions. Then you switch servers and repeat.

### VPN pros

- Low cost: most VPN services charge a few dollars a month

- Useful beyond hotel booking (streaming, privacy)

- You choose which country to test

- Available on most devices

### VPN cons

- One country at a time: checking 10 countries can take 30 minutes or more

- No way to know which country has the best price without checking them all

- Many websites recognize traffic from well-known VPN servers

- Slower connections make each search take longer

- You have to compare final totals, taxes, fees and rate conditions yourself

- Nothing happens after you book, even if the price drops later

- Every hotel, every trip, starts from zero

## How Arbitrica works differently

Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that lives in your browser, not a VPN you switch on and off. It shows up at the checkout when you are about to pay, searches the same hotel from 195 countries and finds the lowest price on Earth for it at a different seller from the one you are on. It validates that the lower price is for the identical hotel and includes all taxes and fees, checks that the price will not suddenly change, and then prepares the booking so you only review and pay.

> Chart: By hand, a VPN checks one country at a time. Arbitrica searches the same item from 195 countries at once.

### Arbitrica pros

- The same hotel is searched from 195 countries for you, at checkout (live arbitrage)

- Validation of the identical hotel, with all taxes and fees included

- The booking is prepared for you, so you only review and pay

- Arbitrica's approach repeats the search after you book, until free cancellation ends, and prepares a rebooking at the lower price (multiple-time arbitrage). The new booking is confirmed before the original is cancelled.

- The same mechanisms also apply to flights, car rentals, event tickets and online shopping

### Arbitrica cons

- Does not replace a VPN for privacy or streaming

- The lower price is always at a different seller from the one you started on, so you may book through a site you have not used before

## Head-to-head comparison

| Criteria | VPN | Arbitrica |

| Countries per search | 1 | 195 |

| Time per search | A few minutes per country | Runs for you at checkout |

| Identical hotel check | Manual | Validated, including all taxes and fees |

| After you book | Nothing | The approach repeats the search until free cancellation ends |

| Booking | You do it yourself | Prepared for you to review and pay |

| Setup | Install an app, pick servers | Personal AI agent (lives in your browser) |

## The math on finding the best price

If each country takes about three minutes to check properly, 10 countries take about 30 minutes and cover around 5% of the 195 countries. All 195 would take close to ten hours for a single hotel, and the answer changes from hotel to hotel and from day to day. Checking every country by hand is not feasible for any booking.

Arbitrica checks the same hotel from 195 countries every time. The same hotel is often 5-30% cheaper from the right country, and research showed that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking with Arbitrica, and up to $3,000 a year.

A real example: Booking.com offered one hotel stay for $1,527.39. Arbitrica found the identical hotel and dates for $1,180.27, with all taxes and fees included. That earned the user $347.12, or 23%.

> Chart: A real booking: offered at $1,527.39, found for $1,180.27 for the identical hotel. Arbitrica earned the user $347.12 (23%).

## If you do use a VPN, check these things

If you want to try the manual route for a trip, a few habits stop a lower number from turning into a worse booking:

- **Compare the final total**Go all the way to the last step before payment. Some sites show prices before tax in one country and with tax in another.

- **Match the rate conditions**A lower price on a non-refundable rate is not the same booking as a flexible rate with free cancellation. Check breakfast, cancellation and payment terms line by line.

- **Watch the currency**A price shown in another currency is only lower if the amount charged to your card, including any foreign transaction fee, is lower.

- **Read the residency terms**Some rates are labeled for residents of a specific country and can ask for proof at check-in. Skip those unless they apply to you.

- **Keep the confirmation**Save the confirmation email and the cancellation terms, in case you need to change or cancel later.

TipStart with the countries you are least likely to guess. The lowest price often comes from an unexpected country, because promotions, channels and exchange rates keep changing.

## When to use a VPN instead

VPNs remain useful for general online privacy and for reaching geo-restricted content. For the specific job of finding the lowest price for a hotel, Arbitrica is purpose-built: it covers 195 countries instead of one, does the checks for you and prepares the booking.

The same applies beyond hotels. Online shopping, event tickets, flights and car rentals also vary by country, and a VPN has the same one-country-at-a-time limit there. Companies booking for teams at trade shows and conferences face the problem at scale, which is why Arbitrica also serves travel managers and operations managers. For the background, read [what geographic price arbitrage is](https://arbitrica.com/blog/what-is-geographic-price-arbitrage.html), [why Booking.com shows different prices with a VPN](https://arbitrica.com/blog/booking-com-different-prices-vpn-explained.html) and [the cheapest country to book hotels from](https://arbitrica.com/blog/cheapest-country-to-book-hotels-from.html).

## Frequently asked questions

### Does a VPN get you cheaper hotel prices?

Sometimes. Different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions, so searching the same hotel from another country can open up a lower price. A VPN can reach those prices only one country at a time.

### How many countries can I realistically check with a VPN?

At about three minutes per country, most people manage a handful. Checking all 195 countries for one hotel would take close to ten hours.

### Is Arbitrica a VPN?

No. Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that lives in your browser. It searches the same hotel from 195 countries at checkout and prepares the booking at the lowest price for you to review and pay.

### Should I keep my VPN if I use Arbitrica?

Yes, if you use it for privacy or streaming. For finding the lowest hotel price, Arbitrica covers 195 countries and does the checks for you.

# What is geographic price arbitrage?

Why the same hotel, product, seat or subscription can cost less when you search for it from another country, and how time arbitrage adds a second way to pay less.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/what-is-geographic-price-arbitrage.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: Hidden prices

## Key takeaways

- Geographic price arbitrage means buying the identical item at a lower price that is available from another country.
- Prices differ by country because each country gets its own mix of channels, contracts, local rates, promotions, currencies and taxes.
- It applies to hotels, online shopping, event tickets, flights, car rentals and subscriptions, not only to travel.
- Time arbitrage is the partner mechanism: live arbitrage searches at checkout, and multiple-time arbitrage repeats the search until the cancellation or return window ends.
- Searching all 195 countries by hand is impossible in practice; Arbitrica searches the same item from 195 countries at checkout and prepares everything at the lowest price on Earth.

Geographic price arbitrage means buying the same item at a lower price that is available from another country. The item does not change: it is the same hotel, the same product, the same seat or the same subscription. What changes is the country you search from, and with it the inventory, sales channels, local rates and promotions you can reach.

It works for far more than hotels. Online shopping, event tickets, flights, car rentals and subscriptions all have prices that vary by country. This guide explains why, shows how it plays out in each category, and covers its partner mechanism, time arbitrage.

## How geographic price arbitrage works

Sellers rarely offer one price to the whole world. A product or service is distributed through different channels in different countries: local retailers, wholesalers, local partners, marketplaces and the seller's own storefronts. Each country gets its own mix of those channels, along with local rates and promotions aimed at that market.

Searching the same item from another country can therefore open up lower prices that you cannot get from your own country. These prices are legitimate and can be booked or bought. Geographic arbitrage is the work of finding them. In practice it has four steps:

- **Pin down the exact item**The same hotel and dates, the same product model, the same seat category or the same plan.

- **Search from as many countries as possible**The lowest price rarely comes from the country you would guess first.

- **Confirm the lower price is real**Check that each lower price is for the identical item and includes all taxes, fees and, for physical goods, shipping and import costs.

- **Buy at the lowest total**Compare the final amounts, not the headline prices.

## Why prices differ by country

- **Purchasing power and local demand.** A price that sells well in one country may be too high to sell in another.

- **Local competition.** Markets with many alternatives tend to see lower prices.

- **Channels and contracts.** Different distributors and partners serve different countries, each on its own terms.

- **Promotions.** Campaigns are often aimed at a single country's market.

- **Currency and taxes.** Exchange rates move, and local taxes are built into prices differently.

> Chart: Different countries get different inventory, channels, local rates, promotions and currencies, and pricing algorithms move rates all day.

Together these factors mean the same item can have many different prices at the same moment, depending on which country you search from. The gaps are not small. In a test of 1,000 hotels searched from 100 countries, 80% of countries showed a lower price than the traveler's own country, and the typical gap was 20-40%. A 2024 NordVPN study found that travel bookings made through US websites came out up to 70% higher than through websites elsewhere (its largest gap was a car rental).

## Where geographic arbitrage applies

### Hotels

Hotels sell through online travel agencies, wholesalers, local partners and their own sites, and each country sees a different mix of rates and promotions. The same hotel on the same night is often 5-30% cheaper when searched from another country. In one real Arbitrica search, Booking offered a hotel for $1,527.39. Arbitrica found the identical hotel for $1,180.27, earning the user $347.12 (23%). The guide to [why Booking.com prices differ by country](https://arbitrica.com/blog/booking-com-prices-different-countries.html) goes into the hotel side in detail.

### Online shopping and retail

Large retailers and marketplaces such as Amazon run separate storefronts for different countries, each with its own sellers, stock, promotions and prices. The same product can cost less on another country's storefront or from a seller in another country, even after shipping and import costs. The total, with those costs included, is what counts. See [how to buy online for less from another country](https://arbitrica.com/blog/buy-online-cheaper-from-another-country.html).

### Event tickets

Tickets for concerts, sports and festivals are often sold through different ticketing partners in different countries, with their own presales and promotions. The same seat category can be listed at different prices depending on where you buy it.

### Flights and car rentals

Airlines and rental companies sell through many points of sale, and the same flight or car can be priced differently when bought from another country's site or in another currency. Fare rules, taxes and insurance terms still apply, so the comparison has to be for the identical ticket or rental.

### Subscriptions and digital services

Streaming services, software and other subscriptions often set a separate local price for each country. Check the provider's terms first, since some limit where a country's plan can be used.

## Time arbitrage: the second mechanism

Geographic arbitrage looks at countries. Time arbitrage looks at moments. The price of the same item changes over time, so repeating the search at many points in time can find a lower price than the one you first saw. There are two forms.

### Live arbitrage

Live arbitrage happens at checkout, in real time. Just before you pay, the same item is searched from many countries at once, so you buy at the lowest price available at that moment rather than the price your own country happens to offer.

### Multiple-time arbitrage

Multiple-time arbitrage continues after you buy. As long as the purchase can still be cancelled or returned, the search is repeated. If the identical item becomes cheaper, a new booking or purchase is prepared at the lower price, and the original is cancelled only once the new one is confirmed. It applies to anything with a cancellation or return window: hotels with free cancellation, refundable flights, car rentals, refundable event tickets, pre-orders and delayed-shipment orders, and subscriptions that can be cancelled. The [time arbitrage guide](https://arbitrica.com/blog/time-arbitrage-explained.html) covers this in more depth.

> Chart: Geographic arbitrage (other countries, at checkout) and time arbitrage (later moments, after you pay).

| Mechanism | What varies | When it runs | Example |

| Geographic arbitrage | The country you search from | Before you buy | The same hotel searched from 195 countries |

| Live arbitrage | Country, at the moment of purchase | At checkout, in real time | A lower price found for the same product just before you pay |

| Multiple-time arbitrage | The moment in time, and the country | After purchase, until the cancellation or return window ends | A refundable hotel booked again at a lower price before the deadline |

## How to tell a real saving from a false one

A lower number from another country is only a saving if everything else stays the same. Before you act on one, check these points:

- **Same item.** The same hotel, dates and rate conditions; the same product model and variant; the same seat section.

- **Full total.** Taxes, service fees, resort fees, shipping and import duties all included.

- **Currency.** The amount your card is charged after conversion and any foreign transaction fee.

- **Eligibility.** Some rates are restricted to residents of a country, and some subscriptions can only be used where they were bought.

- **Terms.** Cancellation, return and warranty terms can differ between countries and sellers.

TipIf a price from another country looks far lower than everything else, check the rate conditions first. A breakfast-included flexible rate and a non-refundable room-only rate are different purchases, even at the same hotel.

## The challenge of manual arbitrage

People who discover that prices differ by country often try a VPN: connect to a server in another country, check the price, switch, check again. It is slow, many VPN addresses are recognized by sites, and it covers a handful of countries at best. Searching all 195 countries by hand is impossible in practice, and repeating that search every time the price might have changed is even less realistic. Our comparison of a [VPN and Arbitrica for hotel booking](https://arbitrica.com/blog/vpn-vs-arbitrica-hotel-booking.html) works through the numbers.

The lowest price also tends to come from an unexpected country. It is not always the countries people assume will be the least expensive, because promotions, channels and exchange rates keep changing.

## Automated arbitrage with Arbitrica

Arbitrica is a personal AI agent that shows up at checkout when you are about to pay. It searches the same item from 195 countries and finds the lowest price on Earth for it at a different seller from the one you are on. It validates that the lower price is for the identical hotel or item and includes all taxes and fees, checks that the price will not suddenly change, and then prepares everything so you only review and pay.

Arbitrica's approach also covers time arbitrage. The mechanism Arbitrica developed repeats the search after you buy, until the free-cancellation or return window ends, and prepares a rebooking or repurchase at the lower price. The new booking or purchase is confirmed before the original is cancelled.

> Chart: Research demonstrated average earnings of $47 per hotel booking, $34 per online purchase and $107 per event ticket purchase, and up to $3,000, $3,000 and $1,500 a year.

Research showed that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking and up to $3,000 a year with Arbitrica, $34 per online purchase and up to $3,000 a year, and $107 per event ticket purchase and up to $1,500 a year. Arbitrica serves both individuals and companies, including teams traveling to trade shows and conferences and the operations and travel managers who book for them.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is geographic price arbitrage?

It is buying the identical item at a lower price that is available from another country. The hotel, product or ticket stays the same; the country you search from changes, and with it the channels, local rates and promotions you can reach.

### Is geographic price arbitrage legal?

Searching for the same item from other countries is a form of shopping around, and the prices found can be booked or bought. Check each offer for residency or usage restrictions, which some rates and subscriptions have.

### Does geographic arbitrage only work for hotels?

No. Online shopping, event tickets, flights, car rentals and subscriptions also have prices that vary by country.

### What is the difference between live arbitrage and multiple-time arbitrage?

Live arbitrage searches the same item from many countries at checkout, in real time. Multiple-time arbitrage repeats the search after you buy, until the cancellation or return window ends, and the original is cancelled only once the new purchase is confirmed.

# Why do hotel prices change daily?

What a hotel pricing algorithm looks at, why prices fall as well as rise, and how to set up a booking so every change can work in your favor.

Source: https://arbitrica.com/blog/why-do-hotel-prices-change-daily.html  
Updated: 2026-10-25  
Topic: Save money

## Key takeaways

- Hotels price each night separately and adjust it as demand forecasts change, because an unsold night cannot be sold later.
- Revenue management systems react to occupancy, booking pace, events, competitor prices, lead time, cancellations and channel costs.
- Hotel prices fall as well as rise: released group blocks, cancellations, short promotions and competitor cuts all create drops.
- Book a refundable rate early, keep checking until the cancellation deadline, and book the lower price before cancelling the original.
- Arbitrica searches the same hotel from 195 countries at checkout, and its approach repeats the search after you book within the cancellation window.

Check a hotel on Monday, check it again on Thursday, and the price is often different. Sometimes it is higher, sometimes lower, and sometimes it changes between the morning and the evening of the same day. Nothing is wrong with the website. Hotel prices are built to move.

This article explains why hotel prices change daily, what a hotel pricing algorithm actually looks at, and how you can use those changes instead of losing money to them.

## The short answer

A hotel has a fixed number of nights to sell, and an unsold night cannot be stored and sold later. So hotels price each night separately and adjust that price as their picture of demand changes. Many hotels use revenue management software that recommends new prices, or sends them straight to booking sites, as fresh data comes in. Every new booking, cancellation or competitor move can shift the forecast, and the price follows.

On top of the hotel's own changes, each booking site can add its own discounts, member rates and promotions. The price you see is the result of both layers, which is why it can change even when the hotel has not touched its rate.

> Chart: Illustrative: revenue management moves the price of the same stay as arrival approaches.

## Hotel pricing algorithm explained

Revenue management systems differ, but they work from a similar set of inputs. The table below shows the main ones and the usual direction of their effect.

| Input | What it means | Typical effect on price |

| Occupancy on the books | How many nights are already sold for that date | Higher occupancy pushes prices up |

| Booking pace | How fast bookings arrive compared with the same point last year or the forecast | Slow pace brings discounts, fast pace brings increases |

| Demand events | Conferences, concerts, sports, holidays, school breaks | Sharp increases around the event dates |

| Competitor prices | Rates of similar hotels nearby, tracked with rate-shopping tools | Prices move to stay in a chosen position against rivals |

| Lead time | How many days remain until arrival | Depends on the hotel: some rise late, others cut late to fill |

| Length of stay and day of week | Weekday business demand versus weekend leisure demand | Different prices for different nights, minimum-stay rules |

| Cancellations | Nights returned to inventory | Can trigger a drop if a date suddenly has more to sell |

| Channel cost | Commission paid to each booking site | Different net prices and promotions by channel |

### Demand forecasting

The core job of the system is to predict how many guests will want each night and what they will pay. If a large conference is announced, the forecast for those dates jumps, and so do prices. If bookings for a normally busy weekend are slower than expected, the system lowers the price to catch up. You can read a longer version in the guide to [how hotel dynamic pricing works](https://arbitrica.com/blog/how-hotel-dynamic-pricing-works.html).

### Competitor tracking

Hotels watch each other closely. Rate-shopping tools collect the prices of a chosen set of competitors on a regular schedule, and many hotels set rules such as "stay just below hotel X" or "never more than a set amount above the market average". When one hotel drops its price, its neighbors may follow quickly, which is why a whole area can move at once.

### Rates, restrictions and channels

A hotel rarely has one price. It has a best available rate, a non-refundable rate, packages with breakfast, member rates, corporate rates and rates for wholesalers. Each can have its own rules and its own changes. A booking site may also fund a discount out of its own commission for a few days. Two travelers looking at the same hotel at the same time can see different totals depending on which of these offers they reach.

## Prices go down as well as up

A common belief is that hotel prices only rise as the date gets closer. That is often true for popular dates, but many hotels lower prices when a night is not filling. Other drops are less obvious:

- **Released group blocks.** Hotels hold blocks for weddings, tours and conferences. Unsold nights in a block usually go back on sale after a cutoff date, which can add supply close to arrival.

- **Cancellations.** Flexible bookings get cancelled all the time. When enough come back for one date, the price can fall.

- **Short promotions.** Flash sales, member weeks and country-specific promotions start and stop on their own schedules.

- **Competitor drops.** If nearby hotels cut prices, a hotel may follow to protect its position.

This is the reason a price you paid last week can be higher than the price on offer today. Our article on [hotel price drops after booking](https://arbitrica.com/blog/hotel-price-drop-after-booking.html) covers what you can do when that happens.

## Does searching the same hotel again raise the price?

Many travelers suspect that a hotel price rose because they looked at it twice. There is little public evidence that hotel sites do this. The more likely explanation is that the price simply updated between searches for the reasons above, or that a limited promotion sold out. Clearing cookies or using a private window is still a good habit, mostly because it logs you out and lets you see the same offers other visitors see.

## What daily price changes mean for when you book

Because prices move in both directions, there is no reliable best day of the week or magic number of days before arrival. A better approach is to set things up so that you benefit whichever way the price goes:

- **Book early on a refundable rate**Choose a rate with free cancellation, so you lock in availability without locking in the price.

- **Note the exact deadline**Write down the cancellation deadline, including the time zone the hotel uses.

- **Keep checking the same booking**Search the same hotel, dates and rate type until that deadline.

- **Book first, cancel second**If the total with taxes and fees drops, book the lower price first, then cancel the original.

- **Go non-refundable only for a big gap**Use a non-refundable rate only when the saving over the flexible rate is large enough to give up that option.

TipTrack the final total, not the nightly rate. A lower nightly rate can come back with a new resort fee or a different tax treatment, and that is not a drop.

## From daily price changes to time arbitrage

Daily price changes are the raw material for what we call time arbitrage: getting the same item at a lower price by searching at more than one point in time. It has two parts.

**Live arbitrage** happens at checkout, in real time. Right before you pay, the same hotel is searched again, so you book at the lowest price that exists at that moment rather than the one you happened to see earlier.

**Multiple-time arbitrage** continues after you book. The search is repeated again and again until the free cancellation window ends. If a lower price appears for the identical hotel and dates, a new booking is prepared at that price, and the original is cancelled only once the new booking is confirmed. Our [time arbitrage guide](https://arbitrica.com/blog/time-arbitrage-explained.html) explains how this works for hotels, flights, event tickets and online shopping.

> Chart: Illustrative: the price of the same hotel keeps moving after you book. A drop before free cancellation ends can be rebooked.

Time arbitrage also combines with geographic arbitrage. At any moment, the same hotel can have a different price when booked from another country, because different countries get access to different inventory, channels, local rates and promotions. Searching from many countries at many points in time gives you far more chances to find the lowest price than one search from your own country. See [what geographic price arbitrage is](https://arbitrica.com/blog/what-is-geographic-price-arbitrage.html) for that side of the picture.

## How Arbitrica uses daily price changes

Arbitrica is a personal AI agent built around both mechanisms. At checkout it searches the same hotel from 195 countries, validates that the offer is for the identical hotel with all taxes and fees included, and prepares the booking so you only review and pay. Arbitrica's approach then repeats the search after you book, within the cancellation window, and prepares a rebooking when it finds a lower price, confirming the new booking before the original is cancelled.

> Chart: Multiple-time arbitrage: the search repeats after a refundable booking. The new booking is confirmed first; only then is the original cancelled.

In one real case, a stay offered on Booking for $1,527.39 was found for $1,180.27, earning the user $347.12. Research showed that people earn on average $47 per hotel booking with Arbitrica, and up to $3,000 a year. You can see how this fits together on our [hotel price tracker](https://arbitrica.com/hotel-price-tracker.html) page.

Daily price movement matters even more when one booking covers many people. A travel manager booking a team into a trade show city can see the same hotel move several times before the event. Arbitrica also serves companies, including teams traveling to conferences and the operations and travel managers who book for them.

## Frequently asked questions

### Why do hotel prices change daily?

Hotels price each night separately and adjust it as demand changes. Revenue management systems react to new bookings, cancellations, events and competitor prices, and booking sites add their own promotions on top.

### Do hotel prices go down closer to the date?

Sometimes. Popular dates tend to rise, but hotels often cut prices when a night is not filling, and released group blocks or cancellations can add supply close to arrival.

### Is there a best day of the week to book a hotel?

There is no reliable one. A safer approach is to book a rate with free cancellation early and keep checking the same hotel until the cancellation deadline.

### Can I get a lower price after I have already booked?

Yes, if your booking can be cancelled without a fee. Book the lower price for the identical hotel and dates first, then cancel the original before the deadline.
